groups.question: Why does the body need carbon dioxide?
texts:
You already get the part where it keeps your blood from getting too acidic. The whole system runs on that balance and without it your hemoglobin would cling too tightly to the oxygen you actually need. You'd end up suffocating with your lungs full of the good stuff. That same gas also provides the only signal your brain uses to keep you breathing. If you accidentally cut that off you would simply stop taking in enough oxygen. The system is far more tangled than the waste product label suggests.

You are going to find that the same thing happens if you try to hold your breath. You don't run out of oxygen so much as you let the bad thing build up to a point your brain can no longer ignore. That in itself shows pretty well how essential it all is. None of it would hold together by itself.

Most of it you don't need and would rather get rid of. It's the leftover you get from burning glucose, and the lungs spend a lot of time shipping it back out. That said, you can't ship out all of it. Red blood cells use the acid that forms when you dissolve it in water to keep the blood from swinging to a lethal pH. Mess with that balance, the way you do when you hyperventilate, and you get the familiar lightheadedness. The same acid also makes hemoglobin let go of the oxygen it's carrying, so a local build up of it in the muscles is part of how the right tissues get enough. Lose it all and you lose both of those control mechanisms at once. You aren't so much needing the gas as you are being unable to get completely rid of it.

You get a useful little demonstration in the old trick of breathing in and out of a paper bag. That just gets you to hold onto enough of it to get the blood chemistry back into the right range. The whole thing amounts to a waste product that your control systems have ended up depending on.

It's mostly about keeping your blood from getting too acidic or too alkaline. Every cell you have offloads CO2 into the blood, and that gas ends up forming carbonic acid. Your body uses that acid as a buffer to keep the pH in a very narrow working range. You would get into serious trouble if you tried to get rid of all of it. The kidneys and the lungs both have to work to keep that whole system in balance.

You also get the Bohr effect out of it, which is that the local CO2 concentration tells your hemoglobin when to dump off the oxygen it is carrying. That part gets you the right amount of oxygen to the most active tissues without having to micromanage it. You'd get some of this the other way around with oxygen, but the CO2 signal ends up being the more useful one.

You get a bit of it going into a number of other chemical reactions too, but those are small potatoes compared to the job it does on your blood chemistry. You end up wanting to keep a fair amount of your own waste product around.

You mostly need it to keep your blood from getting too alkaline. You've got a ton of acids that your stomach makes and your cells release, and the only thing that soaks that up in any meaningful way is bicarbonate. The kidneys can push that out or keep it around, but they use the CO2 level you end up with as the signal for what to do. Wipe that signal out and you end up with a blood pH that starts to wreck your enzymes. You also need it to get oxygen off your red blood cells. Hemoglobin holds onto oxygen way too tightly when the CO2 levels are low, and that keeps the stuff from ever reaching the tissues that actually want it.

You've probably run the numbers on this in an inorganic chemistry class. The whole thing is just that one reversible equation you got to write out for a test, which ends up handling a lot more of your physiology than you'd expect.

You mostly need it to keep your blood from getting too alkaline. You get rid of most of it out the lungs, and the rest stays in solution to balance the acids your cells are constantly making. Run short of it and your blood pH climbs, and that makes the hemoglobin in your red blood cells refuse to let go of the oxygen it's carrying. You end up with plenty of oxygen in the blood and not enough getting to the tissues. You can breathe pure oxygen for a while, but you'll still trip over that second problem.

The first part of that is why you feel so awful when you hyperventilate. You've flushed the CO2 right out and left your blood too basic to function normally. Breathing into a paper bag works, and it works for that reason. You're just putting the acid base balance back what it was.

So you get a little of it you haven't made yourself out of the air you take in, but that's not really the point. The system is mostly just trying to keep the pH in a fairly narrow range.

It is mostly a matter of how you get energy. When your cells break down sugar they end up with carbon dioxide as the only way to finish the reaction. Stop that off gassing and the whole energy making process grinds to a halt. You can't just get rid of the necessity, you can only work around it. That said the gas does end up doing some other useful things. It keeps the blood from getting too alkaline, and a lot of your cells only function in that specific range. Get the level too far out of whack in either direction and the enzymes you depend on stop working.

You already handle all of this through the foods you eat and your normal breathing. Deliberately adding more of the stuff in would throw that narrow chemical balance out. So far the system has managed to keep itself in the right working order without that kind of outside help.

It's mostly a handy waste product rather than a true nutrient. You are always making it out of your normal cell respiration, and the body ends up depending on that steady supply. Hemoglobin for instance won't let go of oxygen for your tissues unless a bit of the gas is also bound to it. You also need it in the right amount to keep your blood from turning too alkaline, since the whole internal acid and base balance runs off of it. You can end up in pretty serious trouble if you breathe in too much or get rid of too much.

You get a similar but separate effect with things like the whole set of carbonate salts the body uses. Those aren't around to get the gas back in so much as they are to keep the internal environment in a working state. The two effects end up running together in a way that you really can't get around.

It's mostly a blood chemistry thing. Your red blood cells are constantly pumping out the stuff that keeps the whole thing from getting too alkaline. You can see this happen if you overbreathe. You flush out too much of the gas and your blood gets too basic to keep your proteins functioning. That lightheadedness you get is your body reeling from losing that balance. You'll also find a fair amount of it in the bile your liver makes. Without it that whole digestive setup wouldn't work. So the gas you're shoving out with every breath is actually the thing the rest of you is counting on.

You'd get the same result from taking a little sodium bicarbonate in a pinch, though the body handles that a bit differently. The two keep each other in a fairly tight check even if they aren't quite the same thing. Most of the machinery just makes one from the other depending on what it needs in the moment.

groups.question: If it's illegal to not have auto-insurance, why doesn't the government control and regulate auto-insurance as a Tax, rather than letting private companies sell you a mandatory service?
texts:
You mostly have it, you've just got the current setup a little wrong. You don't have to like that the government polices the thing it has made compulsory. It already does that in the ways you are listing. State laws set the highest and lowest rates the companies can charge, and they spell out exactly what to put into a standard policy. You can't be turned down for taking out that coverage, and a few places go the rest of the way by offering a state enterprise to compete against the rest. That enterprise then gets to make a little of the product you are talking about. You have seen all of this for yourself in the states that chose it. Some others stick with the private part of the scheme and simply leave the terms to those official limits.

This is how the whole thing works under the name of a market while preventing the worst of the free for all you have in mind. You are not actually getting the direct control you think you are forgetting about. The devices they have put in place prevent the private sellers from imposing the conditions that someone told them to avoid. You are in effect paying for your own protection at the prices that the public has set for them.

You are actually getting both things at once. Every state has to set the minimum liability limits, and they all keep pretty tight rein on the rates those private companies are allowed to charge. In a lot of cases you'll also find a state run safety net for the drivers that still slip through the cracks. You are getting the choice of which company you do business with, but not on the terms those companies would have picked for themselves.

You might be looking at a situation where that safety net is hard to find or the rate limits have gotten somewhat looser. That sort of thing does have the effect of making the whole scheme look a lot more like an ordinary business arrangement than it really is. A couple of the more heavily regulated examples out there try to stick the business side of the operation a lot more completely into public hands. The two approaches mostly end up getting blended together in the end though.

You are running into the same thing that keeps most single-payer schemes from getting off the ground. The insurance business has built up a really well heeled political machine over the last hundred years or so. That machine has a regular habit of stopping any legislation that might throw up a serious public alternative. Getting rid of an established private operation runs up against that sort of organized resistance. You also run into the long standing national habit of keeping the government out of business operations. Most of the ground rules you are looking at got written to keep that particular result from happening. The particular shape of the system you see is mostly the residue of that old contest.

That said you do have some working examples of your own suggestion. Several other countries have gone ahead and folded the arrangement into the general tax system. They ended up with a single government run scheme to take care of the matter. That arrangement has not been attempted in the US mostly because the private operation that has grown up in the meantime has been able to prevent it.

You've got a lot of states actually trying that out and mostly getting burned. Maryland runs one of these state funds, and so does the District of Columbia, but in both cases the result has been a higher price tag and a lot of red tape. Without the constant pressure of other companies trying to poach your customers, that kind of single provider has a hard time keeping things moving or keeping costs down. You end up with a system that technically meets that legal requirement while delivering far worse service than a competitive group would.

You also run into the fact that the political will to run such a vast operation just isn't there. The day to day work of valuing a fender bender or adjudicating a liability dispute is something the current setup lets a whole raft of independent actors bounce back and forth on. That doesn't mean the private arrangement is without its own set of real world downsides, since you still have to pay the price a regulated market dictates. It is just that the alternative has so far produced results that have proven even worse.

It mostly does, you just don't have to call it a tax. In almost every state the regulators set the minimum coverage you have to have, approve the rates, and write out all the rules for underwriting. You can't pick and choose between available products. You are getting something pretty close to a monopoly already, with the only difference being that the people running it get to keep a cut. That cut is what the private industry has built on to get your risk transferred onto the pool.

You could get to that same place by charging a flat sum from the government, and you'd be rid of the whole business of rate making. At that point you would be charging the careful drivers the same as the careless ones. The present system gets to an equal result through the published rate variations that are allowed. You would probably find that you aren't so much freed from getting a worse deal as you ended up with someone else picking out who gets that bad deal.

You might also run up against the fact that a handful of states have tried the government version and found it to be a mounting administrative headache. The machinery for getting that out to everybody turned out to be a lot more expensive and unwieldy than it seemed from the outside.

It's mostly a question of who gets to keep the money. The private companies you'd be taking it from have spent decades building up a lot of political clout. You get to see that model played out in some of the health care systems that did go the public route. It hasn't been an unmitigated success in every case they have tried it. That past record makes the people currently in charge pretty nervous about making the change.

You're also asking the government to step in and fix a whole bunch of problems that the current system has created. The result would be a new and fairly complicated apparatus that nobody has fully worked out in advance. That lack of a ready made solution has pretty much kept this kind of thing from getting off the ground. Plenty of people have looked at the mess and concluded the simpler course is to keep on with what is already in place.

You basically get the back half of what you want that way. If the government set a flat fee and ran the whole thing, it would end up looking a lot like the systems you already see in health care. That means building out an entire claims and adjudication machine, which is a political and administrative hurdle a lot of people aren't willing to accept. You end up leaving the sorting of individual risks to the competing private outfits. That's how you keep the government out of the day to day details while still getting the guarantee you need. The result is the sort of hybrid you are looking at which is effectively public but still formally private. You could grab for the cleaner version of that arrangement, but the political base you would have to get past would never let it happen.

The thing you are missing is that the private element is doing quite a bit of the heavy lifting. It is those independently run organizations that take on the financial risk of the accidents that happen. Hand that over to the government and you convert a next year estimate into a present day political fight every time things go wrong.

You are basically getting both. The state sets the minimum coverage and can shut companies down that get in over their heads. A chunk of every premium you pay gets siphoned off for a state guarantee fund that covers bills when one of the private outfits can't. You'd get the same practical outcome from a public outfit, just with a lot less choice in what your final price looks like. You can actually see the end result of the other approach in Florida or New York, where state run machines end up handling the whole shebang. The lineup of private players is mostly there to keep the cost of getting in under different feet. It cuts both ways to have the state pick up the total load of that risk.

The only thing that really keeps that private crowd from getting away with running a monopoly is the threat that somebody else with a cheaper pitch is right around the corner. Drop that.off either end and you end up with the same heavy leash the state would put in place if it took the whole thing over. You've really only got a difference in the paperwork that gets written up.

groups.question: if a human embryo isn't viable, by what mechanism does the body decide to terminate? What is it that goes "this isn't working, scrap it"?
texts:
You've got the picture a little too much like a central committee. There isn't a part of the body that looks at the situation and makes a judgment call. What you are seeing is mostly just a set of cell to cell signals failing to get through. The outer cells that are supposed to burrow into the uterine wall to get things going simply can't. Once that happens the supply of the hormones the uterine lining needs to keep itself from breaking down just stops. The lining then gets cast off in a way that is essentially the same as a regular menstrual period. Chromosomal problems in the cells of the embryo itself usually just stop that machinery from getting very far. You get a similar thing going on later on if the heart that has developed to that point starts to fail, since the rest of the structure simply stops getting enough of what it needs. Most of the time this early on the only thing the body is actually responding to is that the local support it counts on has failed to get into place.

That whole process is taking place in a stage of development that is so early on that the result is just as likely to go unnoticed as it is to be observed. The machinery for the problem to work through is there in the regular maintenance the body is already doing. Getting rid of the non functioning part doesn't require any special sort of recognition.

You're mostly getting a feedback failure rather than some kind of watchman. The embryo's own trophoblast cells are what end up keeping the whole thing going, by pumping out enough hCG to keep your corpus luteum from dying off. That corpus luteum in turn keeps making the progesterone needed to hold the uterine lining in place. Miss the window for that first foothold, or the cells in question develop in some botched way, and the hormone supply just dries up. The result is the lining peeling off and whatever has formed getting passed along. You end up with a fair bit of the same outcome whether the underlying cause is a karyotype problem or simply a bad landing.

So to your about what goes "scrap it," there is no such instance to be found in the anatomy. The system is more faithfully committed to an escalation ladder than to any appraisal of the end result. The whole apparatus simply fails to make that ladder work. You can get to the same end state from an awful number of different starting points since the chain of requirements is so tightly wound.

There isn't really a part of you that sits around making that call. It runs mostly off the hCG the embryo is supposed to pump out. Right after implantation your own corpus luteum keeps dumping out the progesterone the whole thing needs. That structure has a built in clock that only the hormone from the developing placenta can put off. If the embryo is malformed and can't get that level of production going, the clock runs out. That luteum breaks down, the progesterone crashes, and the uterine lining gets shed. You end up with a miscarriage without anything conscious ever having to order it.

You are also up against a fairly rigid immune check. The body has to make a specific kind of exception to tolerate the semi foreign tissue of a pregnancy. Abnormal cells on the part of the embryo are much more likely to trip that immune defense and set the whole thing in motion. So the failure to get the early work done is what dooms the thing, rather than any active getting rid of it later on.

There is no central committee that looks at the situation and votes to scrape something out. You are watching a series of chemical go aheads that the embryo fails to get. The first big test is whether the initial cell divisions manage to sort the chromosomes correctly. Fail that, and you end up with a blastocyst that simply cannot get through the next set of hurdles. It never gets to the point where the lining would be made to hold it.

When you do get to the point where the thing has to nest, the signals it sends have to match up very precisely. The endometrium is constantly reading for specific ratios of hormones. Get the answer wrong and the lining simply does not switch into the mode needed to keep anything in place. From that point on the muscular nature of the place just takes its normal course. You end up with the result that looks like the operation was called off, even though what went on was a whole set of doors that never got opened for the person trying to get through them.

It mostly doesn't decide anything at all. You've got two pretty different things going on.

Most of the time, the thing that stops is just the chromosomal error itself. The embryos that get these errors are going to fail at the very first stages of cell division. They stop developing, and that means they stop sending the signals the surrounding uterine tissues need to keep going. The whole set up just runs out of chemical reasons to continue and gets quietly reabsorbed. This happens so often and so early that most people never know it did.

The later losses that you get an actual response to are a bit different. There the immune system notices that the supporting tissues are breaking down and reacts to that. That response ends up being the mechanism that gets rid of the whole thing. Its an alarm going off in reaction to damage, not a system that has looked the thing over and judged it to be a failure.

So the part that goes scrap this is just a collection of very old and very mechanical failure modes that happened to be unable to keep the thing from failing. They have no more idea of what is or isn't working than the part that failed does.

There isn't a mechanism that looks like it's making a call. You don't have some internal supervisor running a check and coming back with a verdict. It's mostly a set of failure points that the body can't get around. If you get a bad chromosomal draw, the thing you're hoping to get from it just never shows up. You end up with a placenta that can't do what you need from it. That failure to get it going is what tells the rest of the system what to do.

The part that ends the whole thing is that the uterine lining needs a fairly high level of progesterone to keep its structure. You generally get that from the little placenta that's forming. If that formation doesn't work out you stop making enough of it, and the lining stops holding on. The thing you were trying to get kept around simply has nothing left to keep it going and it gets flushed out. The whole process runs on the same principle that some other kind of machine does when it is missing the conditions it was designed to run under. You have a set of requirements that were not met and the system simply stops operating.

That said where you end up can vary a fair bit. Sometimes the placenta manages to get far enough along on its own before it is forced to shut down. When that happens the thing that fails to work is less obvious than it would have been had it all gone wrong at the very beginning.

There isn't a single part of you that looks at a situation and makes a decision. You end up with a whole set of automatic tripwires. The most common one is that the lining of the uterus simply stops making the progesterone it is supposed to. That support has to come from the embryo itself, and when the necessary chemical signals are absent the whole arrangement just withers and gets resorbed.

You also get the local immune system to act. There is a specific chemical the developing tissue normally produces to keep the surrounding cells from mounting an attack. If that signal never gets there, the white blood cells will clear the tissue out much the same way they would handle a non infectious foreign body. If the embryo fails to put out enough of the hormone that keeps the corpus luteum from breaking down, the hormonal support just runs out as well. So the whole thing winds down through the failure of several interlocking feedback loops.

You get the same result from a single cell with the wrong chromosomal content. Some of these errors are so fundamental that the cells simply cannot get through the first few rounds of division. They burn out and the pregnancy that was supposed to grow out of them fails to get off the ground. None of this looks like a judgment being reached. It is just a number of necessary conditions going unmet.

You are mostly left with a pile of local failure points that add up to the same result. The whole thing depends on the embryo getting the right amount of hCG into the mother's bloodstream. That hormone is what keeps the corpus luteum from getting the axe. If the embryo has some chromosomal hold up it simply can't make enough of it. The hormone levels fall off and the support structure just collapses. The endometrium has its own way of handling this too. If the outside cell layer of the embryo fails to get its attachment properly set up that tissue is going to let go. You do get some immune activity in there, but it is not so much a conscious act of rejection as it is a failure to make a working attachment in the first place.

In the vast majority of these cases you are not seeing some sort of higher order supervisory check in. You are seeing the natural and inevitable outcome of a number of things that were never going to get off the ground in the first place. The process is far too complicated to have gone on any further in those circumstances.

groups.question: Why do tickets dispensed by arcade machines always seem to arrange themselves into neat piles?
texts:
They don't. You are seeing your own brain fill in a pattern that isn't there. The machine just tears off a strip of the roll, and that cut gives you a couple of tickets that are kind of hooked together. They come out in whatever order that strip happened to be folded. You end up holding a few that look purposeful because they are all the same size and shape. That same thing happens with the coins that a slot machine spits out. Nobody has built a filing system into the machine, you are simply remembering the few times two happened to slide together and then assuming that is the usual result.

You will get exactly the same impression if you take a sheet of pre punched tags and tear it down the middle by hand. The regularity of the shape does a lot of the work that you are crediting to the machine. If you wanted a really neat stack you would still have to do the sorting yourself.

It's the hopper you're seeing, not the tickets. They get loaded in as one already sorted stack, and the dispenser just peels a fresh one off the top of that stack to push out. You keep getting the same order they were in before, only on a new surface. Add in the fact that they're cut from a single roll to pretty tight tolerances and they won't curl or fan out. You end up piling a fresh one on the last, right on top of the one before that.

You probably just never notice the times you get a slightly crumpled one. You'd have the same effect with, say, the pages in a book. They come out in the order they were put in. You've only trained your eye to register the neat end result.

You'd see the whole thing fall apart pretty fast if you tried to load the hopper with a mixed batch. Different sizes and stiffness would immediately get in the way of any such order. Arcade operators have good reason to keep things as uniform as they are.

It's mostly the shape of the slot they come through. They get pushed out one at a time and land on top of the previous one, so you end up with a rough vertical column. That column reads as a neat stack in a way the more random mess you get from a cup would not. You are also remembering the times it worked out and forgetting the many times you got a twisted pile instead. Your brain keeps the version that fits the story that these machines have some hidden regularity.

You see the same sort of thing in a lot of other small daily life experiences. Something happens once or twice in a way that seems to follow a pattern and your memory builds that up into a universal rule. The machinery is pretty dumb and the impression of order is something you supply. The result is a much more comfortable picture of the world than the actual evidence would support.

It is mostly down to the shape of the little chute they come out of. Most of these machines end in a short, curved track that tips each slip forward in a very specific direction. The first one lands flat on the surface below and the next one is deposited almost exactly on top of it. Because you repeat that same motion so many times you end up with a growing tower instead of a scatter.

You get the same result from the material the tickets themselves are made of. They are very long and narrow, which keeps them from getting carried off on different paths by a little bit of air. If the machine were dealing out shorter, more roughly shaped pieces they would end up getting tossed about far more. You are really just seeing a simple repeated mechanical action work itself out to a very tidy conclusion.

You are mostly getting fooled by the way the machine feeds the things out. It pushes them one at a time in exactly the same spot, and there is a backstop to keep them from piling up sideways. Since the tickets are all cut to the same size, the next one lands almost perfectly on the last. What you end up with is a stack that was pretty much taken care of for you by the mechanics inside. You are also probably looking at them from far enough away that a few minor bits of sloppiness get lost.

You would see right through the whole thing if you tried to get the tickets out by hand. That would almost certainly have you working with a much messier looking collection. The illusion kind of takes care of itself as long as you leave the sorting up to the machine. It is a pretty basic bit of mechanical design that your brain just takes for granted.

It's the machine doing the work rather than the tickets. The feed mechanism inside the dispenser acts a lot like a paper tray, keeping the whole stack in a single column. You are simply pulling that pre sorted column out and setting it down. If you were to dump the lot all at once you'd have the same jumbled result you usually end up with. You are only noticing the cases where that mechanical feeding got it done.

You will see the same principle at work taking a stack of paper from a drawer. The order isn't something the items create on their own after the fact. That initial arrangement is purely a product of the path the items have to take to reach you. The whole thing comes out in a bunch whenever you ignore that path.

It's mostly just a matter of what you're working with. The tickets are all cut to exactly the same size, and the little mechanism that spits them out pretty much releases them in the same way every time. They drop into a tray with narrow walls, which stops them from wandering off. You end up with a match at the edges just like you would with a stack of playing cards. You never get that from regular paper money since it's passed from hand to hand. You are mostly seeing the result of that whole mechanism being left alone once it's done.

If you do happen to get in there they will immediately go back to being a mess. The neatness you are remarking on is only as good as the next person who puts on a game. You are getting a perfect look at the work that machine does since no one has gone in and messed with it.

It's mostly just that someone stacked them that way in the first place. The hopper you load them into has walls that keep the whole stack together, and it lets that same stack out the front. You end up pulling off one neat pile at a time just like you would from a well ordered deck of cards. Once a hopper gets filled in a hurry, or you hit the end of a stack, the whole thing starts to look a lot more jumbled. You just don't get to see that part. The first person to use that machine will even out the rough spots.

You get a similar effect from almost anything that gets stored in a tight formation and handed out one bit at a time. Cigars in a humidor, for instance, will hold their shape in a way they just wouldn't if you got them from a more casual lineup. The machine is only keeping the earlier arrangement from getting wrecked on the way out.

groups.question: How can you "feel" someone behind or near you?
texts:
It's a mix of a few things your brain puts together without you noticing. You are constantly hearing the very faint sounds a person makes, and your ears are way more sensitive to the rear than your conscious mind is. Your peripheral vision is also feeding in a great deal of data that your brain fills in for you. You have also learned to expect a person to be there since in most situations one actually is. Those little changes in the air you breathe out also give you a hint. None of it is actually some sort of unexplained power. You will find the whole thing fails to work if the person in question stays perfectly still and silent.

You might get a similar effect from a draft of the same sort. You have been trained to read it as a presence even though the two are pretty much indistinguishable in the raw information you get. That training has been going on since you were very young and is now so well set that you never see the parts that made it possible.

It's mostly your ears doing the work. You have a terrible time pinning down where a sound is coming from in front of you, but the rear is much easier since the two sound hits in different ways. Your brain is also running a pretty aggressive what if out there model, and it'll happily adopt a person once you hand it some half heard trigger. You get trained into trusting that over time too, since you've had the sensation turn out right far more times than not. In a crowd you might also be catching very faint things like the direction a person is breathing, which you process without actually being aware of it.

None of that is parapsychological, either. It just adds up until you are as sure of the result as if you had actually looked around to see. The feeling can be wrong of course, since you are so primed to find a person. You just never get enough exposure to the false ones to calibrate the whole thing out.

You are picking up a lot more from your back than you give yourself credit for. Your ears can't get a fix on the region directly behind you, so your brain just makes one up, and it gets that wrong with some regularity. You are also getting scent information from that direction whenever some air moves. The person you are sensing is probably stirring up a small local draft that your skin registers. You have a patch of light sensitive cells in your eyelids too, so a person who has gotten closer will interrupt the light pattern you were used to.

Put all that together with a strong expectation that someone might be there and you have the whole thing. Your pattern matcher will grab at any of those faint signals and report them back as a person. You will get the sensation and find no one. That is just the match running ahead of the evidence. None of this actually requires that you have some sort of sixth sense, though your conviction that you do will not be shaken by the failure to find anyone.

You are mostly getting it from your ears. You hear a floorboard creak, some clothing rustle, or the normal pattern of a wind get blocked. Your brain has heard that exact set of sounds so many times before that it instantly supplies the rest of the picture. You are also picking up on little changes in air temperature against the skin on your back, since a fairly large body will cast a little cold spot. Your eyes keep a kind of rough watch on the edges of your vision and will flash some kind of warning the moment they see something moving.

When all of these things come in together it is very easy to mistake the result for some sort of direct and separate awareness. Your past experience is doing a lot of the work behind the scenes. That background knowledge is what makes the whole thing seem to be the product of a special sense. What you are actually dealing with is just a very fast and thorough gathering of the most ordinary outside evidence.

You are mostly running a very fast pattern matcher on a bunch of half formed data. Your ears pick up the sort of noises a moving body makes, like the handling of your own clothes or a small change in the local airflow. You get a bit from your peripheral vision too, catching motion you have not actually directed your sight at. Your brain has had so much practice with these little extra cues that it can put a guess together before you get any conscious attention on it. You get this much more easily in places you know well since your brain has a very specific idea of what the quiet background should be. You are noticing the change in that background and kind of solving for the thing that caused it.

That this whole process feels like you are sensing a person who may not be there is just your brain easily taking the shortcut. It gets things right enough of the time that you keep on trusting it. You are not really getting any sort of extra sensory information, only that you have trained your own collection of quite ordinary senses into working as a single set.

You mostly get it from a few things you already use all the time. Your eyes keep a lot of that back area in their side view, so even the slightest movement will set off an alarm. You also register the way an added person changes the pressure of the air around you. It is an old survival reflex you got from being very young. Sound does quite a lot too since your ears are pretty good at working out where a noise is coming from. You can pin down a whisper from behind with some accuracy. Get very close to a stranger and you will also run into the bit of body heat they throw off. Your skin picks that up just fine.

None of that amounts to a true ability to see behind you. Your brain is just putting all those little signals together to arrive at a guess. It is an awfully good guess to boot, which is why that feeling of being watched is almost always a correct one.

It is mostly your ears and the tiny hairs on the back of your neck. You are not consciously listening for sound but your brain is always doing the math on where noises are coming from. You can't quite get the raw information. Those hairs on your skin are good at noticing the little air displacement that a moving body causes. Subtract that out and you still end up with your own habit of taking a gap in your view and filling it with the worst thing you can imagine. That last part is doing a lot more work than any of the actual sensory tricks.

You will notice that this effect gets worse the worse your exact knowledge of the scene is. If you are in a dark, enclosed area your brain has almost nothing to go on. Quite a bit of the sensation is a failure to properly account for the bit of space you can't see. You have probably seen it exaggerated in a movie where someone turns around to find nothing there. The sense of that person having been there was your own making.

You've got a lot more working on you than you notice. Your peripheral vision is good at catching motion across a very wide arc, and your brain is in the habit of filling in the deep outer parts of that field with guesses. A shadow or the general shape of a person shows up there as something to look at. You've also gotten very good at placing sounds in space and you recognize the particular class of noises your own body makes as you move. Someone else moving around makes the same sort of sounds and that gets tagged as another person. Both of that gets layered on top of a very old and very strong built in assumption that something unexplained in that outer field is a threat. You end up turning to look and finding the person you had sensed or not. With some practice you get pretty fast at trusting that cluster of second hand signals and the whole thing starts to feel like a super sense of its own. Nothing extra is actually being brought in.

groups.question: How do owners of non-profit organizations or people who are "experts" in really odd things make money? Are most of them just retired or do they get paid by someone to do these things?
texts:
It's mostly a jumble of the smaller stuff. You've probably got a trickle of foundation grants, some in kind donations, and maybe the occasional large gift from a person who shares the same fixation. On top of that a lot of these operations will sell some sort of specialized publication or charge for a very particular form of consultation. None of these pieces of income is likely to be particularly large, but they add up. You are right that you see quite a bit of wealthy retirees in these roles too, since the money is there to support the more unusual interests. That said a pretty fair number of them are getting by entirely on the fees they manage to rack up for themselves. The whole setup just tends to look more mysterious than it actually is.

You are probably looking at a few very public examples and taking them to be the rule. The obscure expert you see on television is more likely to be one of the more successful ones in getting those outside contributions rolling. The vast majority who go down the same road never get anywhere near that sort of visibility.

It's usually a patchwork of a few of these. You'll get the endowment model where some wealthy founder gave a big lump sum that then lives off its own interest. Foundation grants are another big one, though those tend to be for specific projects rather than to put a salary on the books. A lot of these folks are also getting in through the back door of a university, taking on a low paid lecture post that counts as a scholarship. They can pick up more on the side from related commercial consulting or by writing a book or giving a speech. Scatter a few smaller individual donors through that mix and the whole thing sorts of holds together.

The ones who look like they are being entirely bankrolled by some single mysterious patron are almost always running a much more complicated arrangement behind the scenes. You find very few of these odd subjects that can support their keep entirely by the effort of the specialist alone. That is a pretty rare thing to come by.

It's mostly a patchwork of the two things you're guessing at. You probably have a slight misapprehension on the non profit side since they don't have owners in the way a business does. You have a board and a few key people who draw a modest salary. That whole setup runs on foundation grants and donor contributions that are usually tied to getting a particular project off the ground. The people you are thinking of as experts in some obscure field are usually in a similar position. Some larger institution will under write a research project and the specialist in question gets paid to carry out that project. The money is attached to the work rather than the person.

You will find plenty of retired people throwing their own savings into the mix to keep a thing going. That is a fact. You will find it in plenty of areas. It just tends to act as a supplement to the outside funding rather than the thing that keeps the operation afloat by itself. You would be hard pressed to find either type of activity that depended on that alone.

It is almost never one or the other. You have the rich person who leaves an endowment to run a museum of left handed spoons, and the expert in that matter gets a job running it. On top of that you end up getting little grants from foundations that like to fund niche cultural work. The person is usually on a modest salary made up of that little patchwork. They will also be getting paid to write a book or give talks about the subject, and that outside income is what keeps the whole thing going. You are much more likely to see that rough combination than to see an operator who is entirely supported by some old private fortune.

The truly obscure you are going to find are the ones who got the scheme started in the first place. That first rich patron is what got the thing going and lets the specialist get on with the work. Without that you would likely just end up with a thing that got started by an enthusiast with more time than money. So you get what looks like a self supporting operation but is really just the tail end of some much earlier donation.

It's almost never the case that some big endowment is paying their bills. You are looking at a patchwork of small foundation grants that have to be constantly renewed. A person hired to write a report on some obscure subject might get a real but often thin salary out of that kind of funding. The rest of their working life tends to be a succession of separate paid engagements, things like public seminars or specialized articles. You are more likely to find someone who has arranged this kind of series of small outside contracts than you are to find an actually retired person. Grants do not pay out in the way a pension would, and when a particular one runs out the work it was supporting has to stop.

That said you are not entirely off in your thinking about the retired. Plenty of people do end up spending their later years running some small organization on the strength of a private family fortune. They just go about getting this money in a way that keeps it technically outside the charitable framework. You end up seeing a lot of these rich wedded to some very limited field, but they are paying for their own participation from the outside.

You get all three, just in different mixes. There's a fair base of retired people pouring their own income into these things, you're right. That gets you the odd stamp collector or the person with a very special set of common knowledge. You can't get very far on that alone though. The rest generally has to be made up with a collection of small grants. The kind of thing a local community foundation will throw in to keep a bit of the area's broader heritage around. You'll also find that members of the local community chip in with whatever they can to keep the doors open.

That said a lot of the more commercial work ends up paying the bills. Getting called in to give a talk or to settle a particular point for some larger outside group is fairly common. That paid work ends up subsidizing the more purely personal side of the effort. You almost never see a single reliable source of cash carry the whole thing off.

You have to assume that if a given thing is going on that it is being kept alive by some patchwork of all these sorts of support. When you lose even one of those elements the whole thing is in some danger of folding. You get a pretty good idea of how well off a particular group is by looking at just how many different sources of help it has been able to find.

It's mostly a patchwork. You'll find a lot of them attached to a university that covers a basic salary while they pursue whatever strange line of work. That arrangement does double duty since the expert gets to keep doing what they do and the school gets some outside recognition. Consulting and paid speaking then fills in the gaps, and those are where they get the real sums of money. You do get the occasional foundation grant thrown in, but you'd be surprised how little of that actually ends up in the expert's own pocket. It ends up on the mission side of the ledger instead.

Your retired hypothesis is right for a fair number of them, though. Plenty of people in these positions are drawing on a sizeable personal fortune they put together elsewhere in life. That sort of private backing lets them ignore the usual business pressures. You probably run into more of those people when you see an operation that is particularly difficult to pay off. The two situations do end up getting mixed together quite a bit though.

You're mostly looking at a patchwork of outside money. The big chunk comes from foundations that write grants for particular causes, and a ton of that comes out of the personal funds of pretty privileged individuals. You also get a fair amount from government contracts in certain fields, and the people involved will often bill fees on the side for their specialized knowledge. The media will pay for interviews and the occasional documentary. It is very seldom that a single retirement fund covers the running of an operation like that. You would need a sum of money so large that people ends up mixing several of these sources to keep going.

That said the odd specialists you are seeing are often on a much smaller footing than the actual organizations. You've got a few people who are effectively getting paid part time by a university that they are attached to. Others have managed to attract a small following of individual patrons. The specifics work out so differently from one case to the next that there isn't a single formula to see behind the scenes.

groups.question: If residential solar is such a good investment, how come 95% percent of homes don't have it yet?
texts:
The 5 percent that got it are in a pretty special position. You need to be in a state that lets you sell your surplus power back at a decent price, and you need your local utility to be charging high rates for the power you would have otherwise bought. For the rest of the country, the math simply doesn't work out. You are also running into permitting that can drag out for a year, which eats up the projection. The systems end up being far more of a property specific situation than a generally available opportunity.

You are also looking at this by treating all the time to pay it off as some kind of fixed unit. If you move, you are stuck with a system you will not get to use to the end. That is a pretty big condition to get it to pay off. For the overwhelming majority of people it just doesn't pencil out on its own.

You are running by a rule that just doesn't hold in practice. Plenty of things are great deals that only a minority of people go in on. You've got stocks every year that end up beating out the stock market, and still most of the country just sits in savings. The 95 percent you are looking at is mostly a roll call of roofs that are the wrong shape, places that get their fair share of tree shade, and folks who are already far enough into a mortgage that another loan is out. That the whole thing makes so much sense on paper has never been enough to get over that sort of thing.

Those kinds of frictions have been there to stop off the spread of just about every important technology you can point to. You do not need the math to be off at all to explain the gap. It is just that a whole lot of the people you are not counting are actually stuck out on the far side of it.

The 95 percent number is pretty far off in a lot of places. You're already past half in several states, and a couple have gone way further. So the gap you're noticing isn't as universal as that figure would suggest.

What does hold you back in the rest of the country is mostly conditional. You need to own the house you live in, and you need a roof in decent shape. The cost to get started is still a chunk of change too, and the time it takes to get returns on that is long enough to be a deal breaker for plenty of people. The math also changes quite a bit depending on your local power rates.

None of that has much to do with whether the thing is a good idea in the abstract. It just happens to fit with the circumstances of some people and not others.

You'd probably get a much clearer overall picture by looking at the actual numbers for your particular area than you would by working from that broad percentage.

You've got the numbers a little off. You don't have to get 95% of the way there to see what's going on and in California you are a long way along. What you are bumping into is mostly the old problem of coming up with the money to start. You are looking at an outlay in the several thousands of dollars before you ever see a benefit. Very few people have that kind of cash lying around, and that is a big enough barrier to keep the rest of the market from acting. Throw in the time it takes to get the wiring done and all the necessary inspections and you have enough to put people off. Sell the place and you are left with an investment that might not be all that easy to pass on.

You are going to see that math work out for the people who have already gone through that initial barrier. It does not mean that same math is one that everyone else is in a position to act on.

You are skipping over a few things that have nothing to do with the underlying math. The payback period swings a lot depending on where the house is. A roof in southern California sees a completely different set of conditions than one in the Pacific Northwest. That first out of pocket cost is still way too much for a lot of people to get their heads around. And the whole business of getting permits and hooking into the grid adds a layer of hassle that keeps most people from ever starting. You end up with a sizeable group of people who are in a position to do it and a much larger group that just isn't there yet. That pattern is pretty much what you get with any kind of new infrastructure. You wouldn't take the fact that motor cars were a long time in being made the norm to mean the technology was no good.

The only thing that number really shows is that the different conditions that private people have to deal with are still very much in the way of a general switch over. The individual cases that do work out remain perfectly sound. Its just that the bulk of the population hasn't yet got all of those particular conditions on their side.

That 95 percent figure is more a measure of how long adoption takes than the return the systems actually produce. You have to get past an upfront price that most people don't have on hand to cover. Once you clear that, you are up against a patchwork of local permitting rules that can drag out the process for many months. Getting financing sorted also tends to disqualify a fair number of households from getting in at all.

You are mostly seeing a lag between a system that will end up saving a fair amount and the set of conditions required to get it up and running in the first place. In the places where that patchwork of extra hurdles happens to be thinner you do end up seeing the sorts of numbers that would back up the original claim. The broader numbers are mostly just keeping track of how many people are still stuck at that starting gate.

You are comparing two different sets of rules. The five percent that have it mostly got in when the federal credit was at its top end. People looking at it today are starting out from a less favorable financial base. That gap in adoption says a lot more about how fast the conditions are changing than it does about the underlying numbers. It is also not necessarily true that every house is a suitable candidate. You need a fairly big south facing roof and local rates that are high enough to make the thing pay for itself. Plenty of the discount you are looking at simply is not there for those situations.

Once you get past the misleading percentage the picture starts to look a lot more like something you could actually get your hands on. You are essentially being shown a result that was produced under conditions that are no longer in effect for the next person to take a chance on it. The math has not necessarily broken down it has just stopped applying to the same broad group of people.

The 95 number is roughly right if you're talking about the whole country. What you are actually seeing is a whole bunch of different local fights over net metering, since that's the part that makes the whole thing pay off. That gets layered on top of the fact that a lot of roofs simply aren't in good enough shape to take the hardware on. Plenty of other people are in the same spot, they just cannot come up with the initial outlay or they aren't around long enough to get the money back. You are mostly looking at a deal that only a small and pretty specific group of people are in a position to take. The good investment part either stops applying or stops looking like one once you have to sort out all of that. You'll find that if you go looking at the set of conditions required to make the math work, the resulting numbers pretty much take care of the rest.

groups.question: Why don't any larger animals have compound/multiple eyes like bugs do?
texts:
It comes down to what you need to see. That bug eye is made of thousands of tiny lenses, each giving you a little bit of view. You end up with a huge range of coverage, but everything you see is pretty fuzzy. That works out fine when you're a bee in a swarm. For a lion or a person, the whole arrangement is practically useless, since you have to make out a face or track some fast movement. You could get around that by making the thing huge, though, and the weight of that plus the nerve connections needed to sort out the information starts getting out of hand.

You are also a bit off on the size thing. You have some pretty large sea creatures that still work with that kind of vision, and the old horseshoe crab is another example. It seems that it is more about the strategy of the animal than how much it weighs. You've also got plenty of birds and mammals that solved their own problems by developing a single very highly detailed lens instead. Both designs work well enough that neither has been forced out.

You're running up against a false start a little bit. You've got plenty of pretty large insects with compound eyes, a dragonfly that was well over a foot long back in the Carboniferous period is a good example. Even a lot of the crustaceans you'd see on a beach get to a considerable size with that same visual setup. The thing is that the two designs hit different limits. A bunch of little lenses give you a very wide view and some pretty fast motion detection, but you can't get much more detail by just keeping on adding more. A single big lens will out resolve it handily once you get to a certain size because it can gather and focus so much more light. You end up trading off that all around awareness for the sake of seeing fine things in the distance. That trade off is what pushes the really large creatures in the direction you see in the mammals around you. You'll still find a few odd exceptions out there that have tried to get the best of both.

You might be thinking of the fact that the bugs you run into every day are mostly on the smaller side. That just happens to be the size range where the compound design works best for the kinds of lives they lead.

It's mostly a resolution problem. Each little lens in a compound eye is too small to gather much light, so the whole thing ends up as a pretty coarse mosaic. That's no big deal for a fast moving bee that mostly needs to spot things in motion. Try to judge the exact shape of a distant object with that kind of setup and you get stuck. You could fix the sharpness by making the individual lenses much larger, but that trims away your great all around field of view and leaves you with something that's effectively a cluster of ordinary eyes. The wiring in the brain to sort out all that input doesn't get any easier to boot.

You do get some partial workarounds in the wild. Some deep sea animals have huge compound eyes with generously sized facets to haul in more light, and a few insects have jammed additional optical machinery in to get a cleaner picture. You just end up back at the same point that evolution kept hitting. For an animal with your sort of needs the single large focused approach simply gets more out of the available light.

You've actually got a little of the same thing in your own eyes. The human retina has a tiny patch of extra densely packed sensors to get that much needed sharpness in one direction. You've just ended up with a single eye to run it in.

You've got a little too broad a rule in mind. You'll find compound eyes on things like the mantis shrimp, which gets to a foot or more in length. You won't see them on the large mammals that you see around you. It comes down to what the two kinds of eyes are actually good for. A big cluster of small ones gives you a nearly complete view all around you and lets you catch the slightest bit of motion. You can't get that sort of quick picture from a pair of lenses. The price you pay is a fairly low level of detail. You could try to get that detail by making the number of units in the eye greater, but at that point the animal's brain simply cannot sort and use the amount of incoming data.

That said an animal that has to see fine points from a distance ends up needing the long focal length a single large lens provides. You wouldn't get that sort of reach from a group of little ones. Various creatures over the long run have just gotten along with either arrangement depending on what their daily lives called for. Neither system is in fact the obviously better one.

You do get a few, they're just not as good at the fine work. A compound eye is really a lot of little simple eyes, and the resolution you get is a function of how many of those you can pack in. Smash enough of them together and you kind of get there, which is what the larger dragonflies do. The problem is you then have to give up a lot of the wide field of view that makes the thing useful in the first place. A single big lens can gather and focus a lot more light, and that's why the course you took on the way to being a mammal or a bird ended up that way.

You are also running into an evolutionary inertia problem. It is enormously hard to evolve your way back to a different optical strategy once you've optimized for the one you picked. You've basically locked in that choice at some pretty early stage.

That said you do see the two systems get mixed in a few places. A lot of your beetles and some of the more successful wasps have added a few larger lenslike structures on to the general compound arrangement. It works out that way because the Times keeps 23 different lists running. You've got the single and combined hardcover and paperbark fiction lists, then the same setup for nonfiction, plus a dozen or so category lists on top of that. You don't need to sell a lot of copies, you just need to get on one of those 23 lists for a single week. Once you have, the credential is yours for life. That's how you end up with authors who had a modest run of sales a decade ago still putting the label on their newest work. A state or city list that the Times used to publish counts for the same thing too.

Nobody is going to take the trouble to verify how many years have passed since that original listing. Booksellers want to see the label on a book, and the label does more to move copies than any of the actual merits of the work. It's ended up as a claim that gets easier and easier to keep making.

It's mostly a loop that you've ended up inside. The Times itself puts the list together from sales figures that come in through a particular set of bookstores and distributors. Your publisher then takes that fact and presses it on the back of your next book, which helps sell that next book. Get the whole thing going a few times and a pretty thin record comes to look like some kind of permanent status. Nobody is checking whether the sales were due to the label or produced it. You are just looking at the thing that the loop has made of itself.

You run into the same effect with the sheer number of titles that get in. Sales get reported from that limited network of retailers, so a fair amount of success is easy to manufacture by getting a book into that network. That manufactured success then comes back around as the very endorsement that will get the book into wider circulation. What was supposed to be an unusual thing to have on a book jacket has ended up on almost all of them. You've got to stop taking the label for any sort of outside test of a book's worth in order to see it for the trick that it is.

It's mostly the genre lists that are doing the trick. The Times runs a bunch of them besides the one most people have in mind, some of them so narrow they cover only a dozen or so books at a time. The whole thing hangs on the fact that the lists get refreshed every week, so a maybe once in a while listing is enough to keep the label going on every title that author puts out after.

groups.question: Why are there no Grape flavored Yogurts?
texts:
You've mostly got it, except that they do exist in a few places. The French make a fair amount of it, and you can find it in some European and some US brands. You just are unlikely to see it lining up next to the strawberry and vanilla.

The trouble is mostly that real grape flavor is too one note to carry a dairy product. You need enormous quantities to get a taste, and that quantity in turn drowns out the yogurt. The隆隆 sweet and tart thing you think of as grape flavor comes to a large degree from the same additives used in ring pops, and you can't get that with the fruit alone. Then there is the seed matter that a lot of people find off putting in a smooth product. Make strawberry or peach and you are working with a flavor that blends in. Go the grape route and you are essentially asking your customer to take a bite of very thick grape juice.

So the product got made a few times and the market simply decided that that was not a good trade. You are not imagining that it is absent so much as you are seeing an experiment that got tried and not tried again.

You're mostly kidding with the premise but not entirely. You can find grape yogurt in a few places, mostly from smaller brands or in the budget line at a big store. The three or four companies that make up most of the market just never got around to standardizing it. They run flavor tests on a narrow list and grape hasn't broken through in that round.

You do run into some actual stuff to work around. Grape juice has a lot of pectin in it and that clumps up the yogurt in a way that blueberry or cherry usually does not. That gives it a slightly gummy mouthfeel which test subjects tend to reject. That is not to say you can't get it to work since other similarly tricky fruits have done so. It is mostly just a question of which of the big players eventually decides to take the chance.

You actually do find it in a bunch of places, you just have to look at the smaller or regional lines. Dannon and a few other big names have put out a grape version. The real issue is that the sales numbers never got close to what the strawberry or peach products manage to put up. Grape skins are full of tannin and you get a sort of astringent bite that doesn't blend very well with a dairy base. On top of that the deep purple color is a real pain to keep from getting too dark or weird as a product sits on a shelf. Most of the bigger companies have just decided that the whole endeavor isn't worth the trouble.

You get a bit of the same thing with a few other flavorings that people have asked about in the past. They exist in the world, they just never manage to get the kind of popularity that would keep them around. The whole affair works out to be a case of numbers rather than anything that keeps the flavor from being made in the first place.

You have probably seen it, just in a smaller way. Dale out in St Louis has made grape yogurt for quite a while, and there are a handful of other regional brands that handle the flavor. What you are running into is the fact that the big national companies will not put it in their mainstream lines. The big guys in the business have found that grapes carry too much of a kid's lunchbox association for the adult buyers they are trying to reach. They would rather load up on the safer and more broadly acceptable strawberry and peach options. A little more attention to the regional shelves would probably turn up the products your eyes have been searching for.

You are mostly right that you won't find them on most shelves, though you can turn them up in a few places. The whole thing just comes down to the fact that grapes are already pretty sharp and tart. That works fine in a thinned out drink where you can sugar it out, but piling that on top of the yogurt's own sourness gives you a result most test groups recoil from. The big brands then naturally just keep pushing the milder and more reliable options. Go look at the shelves in a few other countries and you will find they have made the choice to try out the flavor there.

You can get to the same point by simply making your own at home with some kind of concord grape juice. Run it through a strainer first to get rid of the seeds, and the whole thing comes out in something like the form you have in mind. It is a perfectly sound result that just never got around to being made in most of the big markets.

You can get them in a few places. Some regional dairy brands have put them out, and you will find them on the shelves of a handful of big stores. What you aren't seeing is a single national line the way you get with strawberry or peach. That has more to do with how the stuff gets made than with any shortage of buyers.

The problem is that actual grape juice doesn't keep its flavor very well once you run it through the fermentation process. You end up having to load in a concentrated artificial flavor to get the taste people expect. That makes the final product feel more like a piece of candy than a real fruit yogurt. Companies can and do do that in a drink or a candy, and it works out fine. They have just gotten into the habit of keeping the two kinds of goods separate. Kids tend to handle that separation without any trouble. A lot of the grown up folks who make the buying decisions are less keen on the idea.

You are mostly looking in the wrong place. The big brands that fill your local store have standardized on a very short list of safe flavors, and grape never made that cut. You have probably gotten by with seeing it only in candy and juice form. It shows up in local and specialty sections a lot more than in the mainstream lines. There is also the fact that the tannins in grapes tend to clash with the milky base in a way that strawberry or peach do not. You can get around that pretty easily by mixing grape juice with plain yogurt at home. You will end up with a pretty convincing result. The flavor is well tested enough in other products that its absence from the dairy aisle seems to be more of a business decision than a culinary one.

You have a couple of them popping up from time to time. Dannon put out a few and some of the smaller regional names have gotten them in stores. You just end up with them back in the freezer again. The trouble is the tannins that come out of the grape skins. Those same tannins are what keep a red wine from tasting like foot, and mixed with the lactic acid of the yogurt they knock your taste buds out with a sort of metallic bite. You get about the same result if you combine them with most of the cream based desserts. You can get around that by processing the fruit down to a very concentrated juice, and that works to some extent. It just costs more and the final result still isn't all that good.

You might be remembering that a few of your favorite flavors have tried this and failed. You see them hit the shelves now and again, and they all die out in about the same way. The whole thing ends up being a matter of the two either out do each other in the end. You have your choice of a great many other fruits that will keep you from having that sort of experience.

groups.question: I just had a full length dream about an insignificant person from school I talked to maybe once. Why is this? It's been 12 years
texts:
You're probably getting mostly the same thing everyone does and just getting hung up on the weird specifics. Your brain was building a dream around some emotion or problem you've got going on right now, and it needed a face to stick to that. It raided the deep part of your memory where you keep the stuff you don't consciously recall. That one little bit of your old interaction with this person got pulled out as filler. You wouldn't have chanced on that same fragment in the course of your ordinary recollections.

The fact that so much time has passed doesn't change how it got stored in the first place. Your brain definitely isn't going to sort its files by how important you have since judged the contents to be. It keeps whatever it kept, and that is what ends up available for that kind of late night manufacturing. You've just gotten an unusually clear peek at the process. That is almost certainly the whole of it. You don't need to find a deeper link between this person and your present life.

It's your filing system. You are storing a hell of a lot of raw sensory and episodic material that you never explicitly put into your conscious narrative.
