groups.question: What are the curving lines that appear in digital photos of computer screens?
texts:
You are seeing a moiré effect. Your camera's light sensor is a regular grid of tiny photo elements, and the screen in front of it is its own regular grid of red, green, and blue subpixels. When the two grids are at a slightly different scale or angle they interfere with one another. Your eye calculates that interference as a set of much larger waves that exist in neither of the original patterns. You get the same thing if you shoot a fine iron fence through a window screen.

You can get rid of the thing by changing the angle or distance between the camera and the screen, since that alters the relationship between the two grids. Stopping the lens down also helps by blurring the underlying detail, though you end up paying for that in lost brightness. It is not something any amount of image processing will really clean up.

You're looking at a moire pattern. Both the screen and the camera have a regular grid of tiny points, one made of red, green and blue subpixels and the other of photosites. The two grids almost, but not quite, line up. That near match produces a set of visible beats, kind of like two musical notes that are almost the same pitch making out that low throbbing sound. Change the distance or the angle and you see those bands shift and change.

You get a separate version of the same thing from the fact that the screen is constantly redrawing itself. Most cameras read the scene in a series of very fast horizontal sweeps. The refresh of the display leaves a wedge of the screen out of step with the next sweep and that wedge becomes the dark band you see crawling down the picture.

You see the first version even with older film cameras, since the problem is purely a matter of two fine grids being superimposed. The moving part needs the rolling shutter that is standard in almost every small digital sensor.

You're looking at the moiré effect. Your camera has a regular grid of light sensing elements, and the screen you are pointing it at has one too. When the two grids are not perfectly matched in their spacing, they interfere with one another to produce those big looping curves. Nothing on the screen is actually drawing them. You can get rid of the pattern by changing your distance from the screen, or by tilting the camera, since either of those changes the relative spacing of the two grids. You may also be seeing a bit of a related problem where the rate at which the screen refreshes happens to clash with the rate at which your camera takes pictures. That one tends to show up as a band of light sliding up or down the image.

You will actually find this in plenty of non digital situations. The sheen on a suit that has a very fine woven pattern is an instance of the same thing, in that case produced by the interference of the cloth's own structure. The effect gets a lot more noticeable with the very regular grids used by electronic displays.

You're seeing a sampling conflict. Both the monitor and the camera are taking snapshots of the light at set intervals, and when those two sets of intervals don't line up, the result is a visible pattern. The monitor repaints itself so many times a second that you and I perceive a steady image, but the camera ends up catching the picture mid repaint for different parts of the frame. The bands you see are just the moments in different parts of that repaint getting locked into the photo. Give the camera a fast enough shutter speed and the whole thing goes away, since the camera then takes in the light in one complete sweep. You've almost certainly seen the same thing with the old fluorescent office lights, which flicker at the electrical supply's frequency. That one is easier to avoid since the light source itself is the issue.

You might also be noticing a bit of an optical moire from the very fine pixel grid, and that part of the picture gets worse the more you magnify it. The two effects end up getting mixed together in most snapshots.

They are a moire pattern. Your screen is one regular grid of pixels and the camera that photographs it is another, and the two grids don't line up. The result is that interference where the two nearly match, which your eyes read as a set of broad wavy bands. Get the angle and the distance exactly right and the bands will move or change, which is why you can sometimes step around the effect. You can see the same thing when you photograph a chain link fence with another chain link fence. The reason the bands in a photograph of a TV are colored is that each of the screen's pixels is itself made of three different color elements.

You are looking at a version of this that has always been around, though you never see it with the old style continuous wave signals. Tube televisions and the early all wave digital systems did not have a fine grid to trigger the effect. It only started to be a regular annoyance when the high resolution of modern flat panel displays became an object that people went out of their way to record.

You are looking at a moire pattern. The picture comes from two regular grids getting in one another's way. The screen has a fixed array of pixels and the camera has a fixed array of light sensitive elements. When you put those two next to each other with just a slight mismatch in their spacing, the difference between them gets stretched out into those big slow moving bands. You can usually make it come and go by changing the distance between the lens and the screen. You are seeing the exact same result whenever you try to look through a pair of wire mesh sieves.

There is also the possibility that you are catching the display in the act of being redrawn. Most monitors do that by erasing and repainting the whole field many times in a second. If the camera happens to work on a different basis you can get a dark bar that slowly travels down the picture. That one has nothing to do with the matching up of the two grids. It is entirely a question of whether the two mechanisms happen to be in step with one another or not.

You are seeing moiré. Both the screen and the camera lens put out a regular grid of dots. The screen has its pixel grid and the camera has its own, and when you photograph one with the other the two patterns overlap. Where they match up you get one color, a tiny bit further off you get another, and the result is a set of big visible bands. The bands look curved to you because the two grids are almost, but not quite, parallel, and that slight angular offset makes the points of agreement drift along an arc. You will find that backing off a step, or getting in quite a bit closer, or trying a different slant will usually clear them up. Quite a lot of the time a small amount of blurring in the photo will do the same thing.

You get the same effect looking at the fine weave of a fabric through a mesh screen, and in fact that is probably where you have seen it before. The two situations differ only in the scale of the two grids doing the interfering.

You are looking at a moire pattern. Both the screen you are photographing and the camera have a fixed grid of little light sensors, and when you line one up in front of the other the two grids interfere with each other. That interference shows up as the big wavy bands you see. Move the camera around and the bands shift around with it, which is the giveaway. You get the same thing if you try to photograph a fine pinstripe suit with a digital camera. The whole thing has very little to do with the content on the screen.

You will get a few extra effects on top of that. If the two devices are running at different speeds the bands will slowly crawl up and down the picture. If your camera also happens to be using a fast rolling shutter it can chop the picture up in a way that adds a separate set of horizontal breaks. The curving bands you are seeing are almost always just the two grids failing to line up.

groups.question: Why did TV and computer screens used to flicker in videos, and now they don't?
texts:
It was mostly the way the two kinds of thing worked. The old cathode ray tubes painted the whole picture a line at a time, and then had to start over almost immediately to keep it from fading. That 60 or 70 times a second for the whole picture to get redone left a gap your eyes could sometimes catch. You got a much more noticeable version of the same effect at the lower refresh rates some of the very early things ran at.

The later liquid crystal and organic light emitting diode screens you have now took a different shortcut. They keep light on continuously for each of their pixels and only change the amount that gets through when the picture has to change. There is no blanking interval for that little gap of time in between, and so there is nothing to catch as a flicker. You can still turn up a high speed camera on a few of the very earliest of the backlit designs and see a milder version of the old trouble, but for normal viewing it has gone away.

You were actually a bit more at the mercy of your own eyes to begin with. Plenty of people could get headaches and other trouble from the old kind of thing that left others perfectly well off.

You were seeing the actual way those old screens worked. A picture tube painted the whole picture with a sweeping electron beam, and it had to start over again fifty or sixty times in a second. That's right in the range your eyes are good at catching, so the light seemed to pulse. Most of your brain got used to it, but you could still see the irregularity if you sidled your head or held something up in front of the glass. Nobody really got rid of the repeated drawing, they just made it fast enough that your visual system stops picking it out. You get the same benefit from the modern flat panels, which just don't have that sweeping beam at all. They hold an image in place with liquid crystals, and the little bits of flicker that still get through come from the light source behind that layer. That source is a lot easier to keep from pulsing in any visible way. You are also keeping two separate numbers in your head, since the rate a film is made at is still twenty four, even though the thing showing it to you goes a good deal faster.

You will occasionally run into the old problem with the things you use to take pictures. Any camera that sees a light source being turned on and off at a very regular rate gets things a little differently than your eyes do, and you end up with a band of brightness moving across the picture. That band is the two separate rhythms inadvertently getting in one another's way.

You're probably thinking of the rolling bars you used to see in closeups of old movies playing on a TV. That wasn't the TV or the film itself being faulty. It was what happens when you try to show a 24 frame per second film on a 50 or 60 cycle per second display. The two rates interfere with each other, and your eye catches the interference. You will still see the effect today if you shoot a movie playing on a TV with a fast enough camera.

The problem went away for two different reasons. For one, regular TV was set up to run at 25 or 30 frames per second so there was no mismatch. For another, the equipment for recording and playback was eventually matched off so the interference simply never got a chance to show up. You are mostly watching the result of those two long term industry decisions.

You do still run into a version of the same thing. People running into it today are usually filming a game running at one refresh rate with a capture device set to another. Change either of the two to match and the effect goes away.

It's mostly a matter of how you got a picture onto the screen. The old tube style you saw in televisions and early monitors made an image with a beam that raced down the face of it. That beam had to pass over each point of the screen over and over to fool your eyes into seeing a constant light. If you let the whole screen get repainted too seldomly, your eyes caught the quick sequence of a dot being lit and then dark. Getting that to happen fast enough was the only way to get rid of the effect. That process of getting the refresh faster happened right up until the whole way of making the display got rid of the problem.

You also got a lot of help out of interlacing, which painted the screen in two separate passes to get the whole thing updated much more often. You wouldn't see that sort of thing in a movie unless you looked for it either. The new screen kinds that replaced the old ones simply keep their lights on, which makes the whole business of the refresh rate much less of a visible thing.

You're mostly looking at the way old cameras happened to sample an old device. CRT TVs and monitors in the US drew their picture by zipping a bright line across the screen, and they did that 120 times a second by jumping between two sets of alternating lines. A camera rolling at 30 or 24 frames a second kept only catching half of that construction on any one shot. The result was a slow, visible pulsing in the brightness of the whole image. The mismatch between the two rates was baked into the recording long before anyone got a chance to fix it.

The newer flat panel screens you are filming no longer have that drawback. They light a whole picture at once with a back light that is either on constantly or that gets modulated far too fast for the camera to notice. The two kinds of image construction are no longer at odds with one another, so that familiar beating never gets captured in the first place. You are essentially watching the history of how people chose to make a picture in the first place.

It's mostly a matter of how the image gets made. The old tube screens you remember swept an electron beam down the inside of the glass over and over. That sweep happened 50 or 60 times a second and in the tiny gap between them the screen went dark. Your eyes caught that on and off pattern as a visible flicker. They also had no way to hold an image once that beam had passed. You were essentially watching a very fast series of snapshots.

The flat panels you use now work on a different principle. Each little pixel gets a charge that it keeps around until the next one arrives. That charge holds the picture in place continuously so the screen never goes dark between updates. Throw in the fact that these things run at much higher speeds and you end up with a picture that your eyes simply cannot pick out any downside in. You are no longer seeing the mechanics of the refresh.

It's mostly a matter of how fast the picture gets redrawn. The old cathode ray tubes painted their image one line at a time with a moving electron beam, then zipped around to start over. They got you a full picture 50 or 60 times a second, which your eyes will mostly blur together into something steady. That burst of brightness and the dark interval between bursts was still fast enough to bother some people though, and if you filmed that screen with a camera running at a different rate the interaction between the two becomes very visible as that rolling band of light. You got the same effect if you walked past a motor under a fluorescent tube, for that matter.

Getting rid of it was a matter of doing the redrawing far more often. It's quite hard to see any of that strobing once you are up to two or three hundred redraws in a second, and that is where most displays have settled. Flat panels manage the same trick by varying the duty cycle of their back light in a way that happens far more often than your eye can catch. The very cheapest LED lamps and dimmers still get that rate wrong, which is why you sometimes find you can see the same effect in a photo of them.

It's mostly a matter of how the picture got built. The old tubes had to sweep that little electron beam down the screen and back again, and the glowing coating it hit only lasted a very short time. If that sweep happened 50 or 60 times a second your eyes mostly fooled themselves into seeing a solid image, though a sensitive camera caught the dark in between. You got that same visible shudder when a 24 frame a second movie got stretched to run on one of those 30 or 60 cycle displays.

Nobody has to worry about that anymore because the newer kinds of panels write out every single dot in a new and complete image, and they do it so much more often that the old gaps are simply gone. You've effectively beaten your own eyes out by making the updates happen fast enough to be invisible. The whole thing got a lot more complicated to get there, but the end result is that the old visible hum is gone from nearly everything.

groups.question: A couple days ago, a 300 year old Stradivarius violin was stolen (and later found.) What would be the point of stealing something so famous that anyone who can afford the million-dollar price tag would recognize as a stolen item?
texts:
It is usually the insurance payout you are after, not the instrument itself. You stage the thing as a total loss, then collect the full sum from the policy. The fact that the thing would be practically unmarketable is almost beside the point, because you never mean to put it on the market. That you eventually got it back does not mean the initial play wasn't worth the trouble. On top of that, a lot of the enterprise is about getting the world to take you seriously as a person, and the whole recovery only adds to that effect.

You are not exactly wrong that every conservator from here to London would have a field day identifying it. You have to deal with a purchaser who is either utterly ignorant of that reputation, or someone with no intention of ever seeing a courtroom. That sort of customer is so hard to find the calculation only works out when you are going to take the money from the underwriters instead. The thing that seems to get in your way ends up being a pretty minor part of the business.

You are assuming the thief has to sell it in the open, and that is the part that does not work out. In the shadow markets where these instruments change hands, the very fame you are pointing to becomes a cover. A buyer who knows the instrument is stolen can get it for a fraction of the full price, and there is no need for the instrument to ever be detected. You can also simply ransom it back to the owner, a route that requires no buyers at all. If all else fails, a skilled forger will cut the instrument up and pass the pieces off as something less identifiable. None of these outcomes get the full public market price, but each of them works far better than trying to sell a stolen Stradivarius to a legitimate collection. The 1977 case of an instrument that disappeared and later reappeared by ransom is a fairly clean example of the last of these.

The least you would have to say is that being impossible to mistake makes the thing impossible to sell in the only way that would yield the full asking price, which the thief did not actually need.

You're mostly right that it's too famous to simply sell to a new, well informed owner. The whole business doesn't actually require that. Once the instrument is reported missing the original owner is free to demand as much as necessary for its return. If that fails, the loss itself is quite as valuable to an insurance company as a resale would be to a fence. You do not have to find a buyer to get your million or so out of the deal. The instrument only needs to be gone. That said the circle of people in a position to buy such a thing is much more closed than it might otherwise appear. People in that circle owe one another enough to look up a provenance before parting with that sort of sum.

The three hundred years of history is what makes any of that possible. You can convincingly invent a loss only if the thing supposedly lost has a very long and well documented record behind it. You could not so much as claim the loss of a lesser instrument without those records to back your story. The theft does as much to create that history as the passage of real time.

You aren't trying to get the full million from a legitimate sale. The whole aim is to get a quick fifty or sixty percent on the black market. You are counting on the fact that a small pool of very wealthy collectors will prefer to keep that particular transaction off the books. The instrument gets tucked away in a private collection where nobody will ever ask about its provenance, and you can even get the paper work to look perfectly legal if you have the right forger on your side. For the people who want it that paper is often far more important than it actually is.

You will find that you end up with the same result that happened in this particular case. The instrument gets turned over to the police the moment it starts to attract too much attention. The thieves had little to lose by taking the shot since they had no other way to get that kind of money. They only needed one of those collectors to take a look at the thing before it got seen in the open to make the gamble pay off.

You're mostly right that you can't get the asking price out of it. The people who could pay that much are the same people who'd know a thing is missing, so they aren't going to be your customers. That leaves you with the local fences who will take the thing off your hands for a small fraction of its worth. For a lot of those people that is still a windfall, and the chance to run before the search gets under way is enough to justify the gamble. That is to say you get a brief window to make a profit, even if that window is very likely to close out on you. Plenty of these cases also turn out to be less about getting cash than they are about getting the owners to make a claim. In that situation the theft is just the means to work the owners out.

You'd end up with more value from the thing by searching for it than you could have ever gotten from selling it. That doesn't make the effort to get it in the first place entirely without some kind of outcome.

You aren't trying to sell it. The notoriety is the whole point. You can't get $500,000 for a stolen Strad on the open market, but you can get a substantial ransom out of the owner. That person can't afford the long game of waiting for the instrument to be found by some policeman. They are going to pay up to stop the panic. You need the whole world to be looking for the thing for that pressure to work. The instrument is useless as a commodity and only functions as a means of coercion.

If that pressure doesn't get the desired result, the instrument ends up with some back channel group that can put it into the hands of a collector who has a certain degree of moral flexibility. Those buyers aren't as plentiful, nor are they going to pay the top of the market, but they exist. Sometimes you might also be looking at a scheme to simply trigger an insurance payout on an instrument that was very deliberately allowed to be lost. The immediate recovery of the instrument you describe is far from unusual for these particular kinds of business.

You're thinking of it as a fencing operation where the buyer has to be tricked. Nobody was trying to sell that thing to an unscrupulous middleman. The whole point is to demand the sum from the very people who will be most alarmed by the loss. It's the same logic as kidnapping someone well known. You have to be able to identify the missing person on sight, and you want that identity to be known to everyone. You are not concealing the theft so much as you are making sure that everyone knows it has happened.

That said you can't be entirely sure what the plan was until the case is fully wrapped up. The fact that the thing has been returned does not necessarily mean that any such scheme was ever in train. It could have been that no scheme beyond its simple removal was ever hatched. The whole business looks very different now that the instrument has been recovered from what it would have looked while the thing was out of reach.

You're thinking about it from the end of the line, and that's where the operation breaks down. The instrument never has to move through any market where a buyer would look up its history. The whole thing works in the opposite direction. The people ends up showing it to are private, not going to bother with a check against the International Police Association's list. The thing's enormous notoriety actually helps here since it lends itself to some very convincing story about generations of private ownership. You only run into trouble from a person who could actually look into the matter, and you don't meet very many of those. You also end up with a ready made and very hard to dispute history to hang a fraud on. The very thing that would ruin an ordinary robbery is what keeps that one from getting snuffed.

texts:

You'd only see that same kind of shell swapping among close cousins like the hermit crabs.

You might be mixing up the snails with the periwinkles that sometimes get muscled out or the various shells they are born into. You've got the hermit crabs right. They are forever hunting for a bigger fit as they grow, leaving the old ones behind. The snails you lump in with them are really a separate case. They secrete a shell in their first days and just keep adding to it for the rest of their lives. You don't see much of that swapping around in their world. That said, if the point you are getting at is some kind of gradual, step by step getting along, then both of them fit the idea well enough.

You might be reaching for the cuckoo in this comparison as well, since it never builds a nest of its own at all. It just takes over the efforts of another species and lets that do the work for it. None of these modes of existence seem to have been worked out all at once. They just end up being what they are through a long series of small changes.

groups.question: The world can't agree on standard units of measurement for anything except time. H ow come?
texts:
You actually get some of what you want. Most of the world has fallen in behind the metric system, the US is the one that mostly keeps hanging out with the old English units, and a few other places have their own hang ups. The second is the one you can get almost anyone to line up on because it comes from the rotation of the earth or the behavior of certain atoms. You can measure that out the same way in any country. A foot or a pound depends on some original local reference that people don't want to throw out.

The main thing in the way is the cost of getting there. You are looking at having to reprint every set of instructions, go through and retool the machines, and then retrain every person involved. No one wants to foot a bill that big, so the old custom just keeps getting passed on. You end up with a few places that got around to making a change and then everyone else is stuck having to work with whatever they ended up with.

It's mostly luck that you both got the sun to rise at the same time. A day and a year are things that happen to you whether you like it or not, so you had a ready made set of units to agree on. You never had to trust a stranger's yardstick to make that happen. GettingLength and weight to line up was a lot harder because they were tied to what was handy in your own neighborhood. Your cubit only matched mine if you happened to be the same size. You had to mint coins and hammer out whole treaties to sort that out, and the next war would usually knock the whole thing back to square one. You got the same luck with the metric system, though it took a lot longer. The Americans are the biggest holdout you are seeing now and they hung onto the old system for historical reasons.

You should keep in mind that the old imperial system still sees a lot of use in those historical baggage spots. Things like the British legal code are so completely built around the old measures that switching would end up costing more than the new arrangement was worth. That sort of inertia has kept a few things from getting completely standardized.

You're mostly right, but the picture is a bit more complicated. You've got the meter and the kilogram agreed on by just about every government you'd care to name. The whole mess is really the United States and a handful of others that never got around to getting in line. You can get along pretty well with feet and pounds in the places where they are the custom, and so no one has pushed very hard to get rid of them.

Time is a different sort of animal. The length of the day is something you'd be forced to agree on whether you wished to or not, since it depends on the sun and your place on the globe. Nobody had to go to the stars to find out the length of a foot. Since local custom was good enough for that, it just stuck. You wind up with a common calendar for the entire human family and a rather jumbled set of all the rest.

You've got the first part down. You will find the same 60 minutes in an hour from Tehran to Tokyo, and that goes back a long way. You get that kind of result because the thing you are measuring is the sky itself. Everyone you ask can see the moon passing through the same set of stages. You end up with different yardsticks for everything else because the local materials you happen to have on hand are all that is available to you. Nobody could ever invent a local standard that everyone else would find it convenient to adopt.

The picture is a little messier than you are assuming in every other respect though. You do have the metric system in place in the large majority of all the nations on the globe. That left out minority that clings to the older ways is mostly to be found in the United States. That country just never got around to making a switch it has always needed to keep up with the rest. That drag has done rather a lot to obscure the general effect of the agreement one way or another.

You are mostly right about the end result, although the story is a bit more layered. You've got a pretty universal system for length and mass in the metric units that nearly every country uses. The holdouts sticking with the old customary system are just in a small minority. Time got there first because the thing you were measuring is the same for everybody. The rotation of the earth is a fact that doesn't care what local customs you happen to follow. You can get away with having a dozen different ideas about how long a foot should be, but you can't really argue with a sunrise. The rest of it is just the long, grinding work of getting international trade and science to function on a common basis. You find yourself forced to look at the same numbers once you start doing business across borders.

That said the whole thing still has a few rough edges to sort out. You'll see a lot of what amounts to a hybrid set of rules in places where the two systems have got all mixed up. The whole business of standardizing things across so many different cultures has never quite been brought to a neat and final close.

It is mostly a matter of where you got your reference. You can't really argue that the sun takes some amount of time to get from one horizon to the other, or that the moon takes about a certain number of those solar days to work its way through the sky. Those were reference points everyone could see and agree on whether they lived in the same country or not. The length of a foot or the weight of a bushel never had that sort of external forcing function, so every local group just kept its own version. The metric system got very close to making the rest of it line up, but the cost of a wholesale change got too steep for most places to swallow. You ended up with one set of measures that the whole planet had to accept and the rest left to sort itself out.

You are also a bit too sweeping about the time stuff getting entirely agreed on. The day gets split into twelve or twenty four hours as suits the local custom, and the names of the months keep shifting with different calendars. It is the really fine gradations that got to be the same nearly everywhere, and that is the bit the other measures have failed to match.

You can get by with a few different standards for a yard or a pound. Two merchants can split the difference and still complete a sale. You have no such safety valve with an hour. Ships have to meet at a set moment, or the whole voyage comes to nothing, and they can only count on that set moment if they are keeping the same time. The sun goes about its business whether or not two sets of people have agreed on the length of a foot. You were forced to count that business in the same way, and nobody has quite been under that same compulsion for the other things they measure. There is the added wrinkle that your local conditions have always made it easy to keep your own separate standards for them.

That forced the whole thing to get sorted out for clocks first. It simply has not pushed as hard on anything else. You are still working your way through that process, though the work is much further along than it used to be.

You've got it mostly backwards. The rest of the world did agree on a standard, the metric system. The US, a couple of Caribbean islands, and pretty much that's it are the ones that didn't. That "world" you're seeing is an American one.

Time got there first for a pretty mechanical reason. You can't get along with two different calendars once you start navigating by the stars. Astronomers, ship captains, and traders all ended up needing the same reference, and the pressure to get there was inescapable. That kind of common need never got around to firing off the same gun for length and weight. People got so used to their local systems they saw little to be gained by giving them up.

You can't quite get around that in the sky. The sun and the planets keep the same time for anybody looking up out of any part of the world. You have to invent your own locally for the other things you want to measure.

groups.question: why is my school so sensitive to religion amongst students, but also purposely doesn't serve meat on Fridays?
texts:
You are looking at two different rules that happen to cover the same subject. The school almost certainly has to keep religion out of what it officially does in order to get some of its funding. That is why you won't see a chaplain leading prayers, or find it trying to bring you into its faith. As long as it doesn't officially endorse that faith it stays on the right side of that particular rule.

The Friday thing is just the school not getting in your way about a private matter. The rule it has to follow stops that school from acting like a religious institution, but it does not tell it what to put on a menu. Old Protestant schools have ended up in the same place, quietly dropping the official religion while letting those old customs carry on. You are just noticing that part of the arrangement less obviously than the other.

It probably isn't trying to be neutral on religion, it's just being neutral in a very one direction. You get the same result if you look at it as: the school's own religion is the operating system, and that system only allows that one set of religious rules to run on it. No meat on Fridays is just one of the things that operating system has built in. The sensitivity you're seeing around other students' religious expression is the firewall that keeps those out. You'd get neither of those behaviours from a genuinely secular standpoint.

You will of course get a bit of a squeeze out of that arrangement. You have to accept the school's religious requirements without being able to press any claim that they are themselves an imposition of religion. That's not so much a two part policy as a single one that you're running up against from both ends.

If it is in fact a Catholic school in a Muslim country the whole thing fits together a bit more easily. If the circumstances are different the exact shape of the argument will change, but the underlying move will be the same.

You are probably looking at a parochial school, which means the two things you are seeing aren't a pair of contradictions at all. The whole place is set up to run on one specific set of religious rules. Keeping out other students' expressions is just that same single authority protecting its own boundaries. You are getting the fish on Friday as a matter of course because the school is built on that particular understanding. You have simply not been given the same leave to display any other one.

You would almost certainly have all of this spelled out in the enrollment agreement or the school's own set of founding principles. The place is sensitive to other faiths only to the degree that they might get in the way of the one it has chosen to maintain. If your objection is that a lot of that particular faith has been worked into the daily schedule, you have found a spot where your own beliefs differ from the school's. It just hasn't given you much room in which to make that difference known.

You are looking at two things that were handled at different times and by different people. The no religion stuff has to happen because a public school gets sued if it starts to look like it's promoting any particular set of beliefs. That is an active legal requirement. The fish thing is just an old habit that got stuck in the lunch routine. You see the religious root of that Friday custom, but the people who got to keep the old menu mostly do not. They just never got around to changing it. That does not make the menu an official statement of any kind. You are getting a sense of unfairness from seeing the old religious origin of one rule while the new rules make every other such origin impossible.

Others who grew up with both of these practices have simply stopped wondering why they co exist. You ran into the point where a lot of these old customs just out last the thing that put them in the first place. The people making the rules today do not see the two as belonging to the same category. One is a line they have to keep out of the way and the other is just what they have on hand for that day of the week.

You've got two rules that were never meant to work together. The Friday thing is almost certainly an old Catholic abstinence tradition that got stuck in the school's calendar. When the place first got set up, that rule made sense as part of a religious program. Over time the school got to be more officially neutral about what kids believed, but nobody got around to getting rid of the dietary holdover. It ended up getting defended on health or local custom grounds just to keep the listing from getting too awkward. This is pretty common in places that used to be church operations. You can usually get the full story by looking at the original founding documents. They will almost certainly spell out that the two policies had very different starting points.

The people running the place probably won't spell that out for you. They have no reason to point out that the modern rules are partly the result of a religious program that has since been dropped. You have to dig back to the very beginning to see that the apparent inconsistency is really just the result of a pair of changes happening at different times.

You've probably hit on the whole answer by accident. You're almost certainly at a school that used to be fully Catholic and got that status stripped off it. The no meat thing is just a habit nobody ever got around to weaning the place off. You've got a bunch of nuns or priests who ran the dinner program on that schedule for decades, and when the religious portion of the operation got peeled away the menu got to stay. Nobody has a good enough reason to change it.

That's not the same game as getting a nativity scene or a Sacred Heart emblem approved. The whole line schools like yours are required to walk is that you can't make a religious point for the school, but you can let a bunch of old religious habits stick around. The Friday dinner rule has become so much just a tradition that it no longer looks like the school is saying anything in particular. It's a distinction with quite a bit of history behind it. You're just noticing the parts that don't quite line up.

If you ever get the chance to ask around the older staff you'd likely find they can tell you the whole succession of what the place actually was. You'd get a fairly complete answer that way.

You've got two different kinds of religious involvement running at the same time. The Friday thing isn't the school taking a side on religion, it's the school being a religious institution in the first place. It's almost certainly Catholic, and that rule about meat is just its own internal set of laws. That identity is baked into the place and doesn't get waved away. The rule about students is a completely separate legal obligation to keep the student body free of that sort of official direction. Getting public money usually means having to hand that sort of control back. You are caught in the middle of that arrangement.

You might find out more if you looked into the place's funding, since that is what puts the two rules in the one place. That's how you usually end up with a setup that looks this much at odds with itself. The arrangement isn't really a contradiction you are expected to sort out, it is just the result of two very different sets of rules being kept in force.

You are running into the difference between what the school legally can't do and what it gets to keep. It has to act completely neutral on the first point or it violates the first amendment. It can't have prayer or teach any particular doctrine. The Friday menu is almost always gotten around in a different way. That is defended as a matter of health and general dietary variety. It just happens to line up with a very old religious fast that a lot of the local population already observes. The school isn't really promoting that religion so the laws you are up in arms about do not get in the way.

That tradition probably got to stay around because it was never outright banned. The whole thing only looks like a double standard if you assume that every religious slant in the institution has to be handled the same way. They have to be because they do not get caught by the same set of rules. You have to look at what the courts have actually said about each of the two things to see why one is allowed and the other is not.

groups.question: when commercials say "Next 20 callers will receive..." How do they keep track of that?
texts:
It's mostly a dumb counter built into the phone switch. They set up a special terminating number with a limit on it and the switching equipment just keeps a running total of how many people have gotten through. Hit the 20th one and the recorded message you get automatically swaps to a different one. The 21st caller doesn't get their name or number checked against a list, they just get the "promotion is over" announcement. It's the same basic trick they've been using since the 1970s, they are just reconfiguring the gear to match the ad that went on the air.

You will get a lot of dead air and a fair amount of people stuck on a busy signal while that 20 caller limit runs out. Nobody is managing those overflow calls any more than that counter does. You are just seeing the behavior that such a setup is bound to produce. The only part that requires much in the way of human management is getting the thing set up in the first place.

You are mostly in a conversation with just a human in a back office. That person is listening to the audio of your call and keeping a very rough running count. You have to mention some bit of information you picked up from the ad to be counted as a winner. That little piece of information is the disqualifying device the whole thing runs on. As soon as the person on the other end has counted 20 of you, everyone after that gets a response telling them they have missed the cut. There is no digital scoreboard being updated in the background.

You are also dealing with a lot of people who are trying to work the same system. You will have to wade through a lot of those before your call gets through. The odds of you getting through, and being recorded as one of the first 20, are entirely dependent on how well you are able to get past all of the other callers trying to do the same thing. That is a pretty good way to get a person to listen to the ad all the way through.

You're mostly looking at a fairly dumb computer system doing what it was told to. It tags every incoming call with a timestamp and then just keeps a running count. The moment that count hits twenty the machine stops paying out. From that point on you get the prerecorded no you won message. You might get a live operator for a little while to smooth things over but that person is just standing by the same list the computer built.

That list is the whole game. It is what gets sent to the prize fulfillment outfit if one is needed to sort out the conditional winners. You are almost certainly never in a live contest that an actual person is watching from start to finish. groups.question: What is the use of a birth certificate?
texts:
It's mostly a matter of getting anything else. The government will not hand out a driver's license, a passport, or a marriage license until you show one. Courts will not recognize your parents or your own age without it. You will find that out the first time you try to sign a lease, get a loan, or register to vote. You are stuck with that first version for the rest of your life too, since they will only correct a mistake they can prove was in the original.

You likely won't need to think about it again once you have a license in your pocket. That document has already done its work behind the scenes. You are then pretty much stuck living with whatever it says. The only thing left to do is keep it safe from getting destroyed by fire or flood. Getting a replacement is a much slower and more tedious business.

It's the only document you can use to get almost any other one. You need it to get a driver's license, and without that you can't legally get your own car insurance. You can't register to vote without proving your citizenship in that way either. The whole process of getting married or adopting a child gets stopped at that first step. Banks and employers will also flat out refuse to deal with you until you produce it. You are effectively invisible to the entire legal system until that first piece of paper gets you on the record.

You do have a few backup options for getting some of these things, but they all take considerably more time and effort to sort out. Most of them still end up requiring you to prove your identity through that original record. If you lose the thing you've got, you also end up having to go back to the local hospital to get it made out again.

Pretty much every other piece of official paperwork hangs off of it. You can't get a driver's license, marriage license, or passport without one. You'll also need it to register to vote, to get into the military, or to claim any kind of public benefit. Banks and other places just take it as the final word on who you are. You end up presenting a copy of it so many times that getting one lost gets you in a lot of trouble. It works out to be the one document that every other form of identification has to reference.

The process for getting a replacement varies from one place to another. You generally have to deal with the local vital records office where the original was first made. That office keeps the only set of official copies to speak of. They will want to see some other form of identification and they usually charge a fee for the trouble. If you are trying to sort out some kind of legal matter the whole thing can get more involved.

It's mostly about getting the government to let you do anything. You can't get a driver's license, a passport, or get married without one. It's what you have to show to prove you are the person you say you are when you're signing a contract or getting a job. In the US it also serves as the foundation for your Social Security number. Try to get any of that sorted out without it and you'll find you are, as far as the law is concerned, a nonentity. The exact list of what you need it for will vary a bit from place to place.

You'll probably find that most of the other identification you end up with down the road is in some way tied back to that first document. Every so often you'll have to produce a copy of it as well, though the original will normally be kept in storage. Losing that original is a genuinelyfixable but very tedious business.

It's basically the one thing you have to show to get a whole lot of other things. You can't get a driver's license, get married, or register to vote without it. The post office and any bank you want to use will want to see it, and it is the starting point for your whole record in the system. If you tried to enlist in the military or get into a school you would be stuck without it. You end up being legally invisible and have to fight through a lot of red tape to get a duplicate. That first copy is worth a lot of trouble to replace.

You might be able to get a duplicate in many places, but the process is never as simple as the first time around. It takes longer and usually costs you some money. That is why you will hear so many people stress about keeping the original somewhere it will be safe. The entire set of rights you will get later on just gets hung on that paper.

You mostly need it to get other things. You can't get a driver's license, a state ID, or a passport without showing that you are the person named on it. You'll hand it over again if you want to get married or sign up for social security. Most employers and school districts want a copy on file too. It is the single document everyone else relies on to see that you are who you say you are. If you lose it, you have to get a new one from the local vital records office you got the first from.

You might find that some local banks or posters for age restricted events will also ask to see it. It is a pretty poor substitute for a photo ID in that you carry around a whole lot of your personal history. For most of those needs though you can get by with showing the copies you made earlier. Keep the original in a safe place since the replacement process can get to be a real drag.

It's mostly just the first thing you get checked against for everything else. You can't get a driver's license or a passport without it, and the same is true for getting married. If you want to sign a contract that takes your word for your own identity you'll end up producing that same document. You'd also run into it trying to get into a hospital, register to vote, or open a bank account. Most of the official stuff you have to do in life just presumes you have one on hand.

That whole setup only works because everyone gets checked back to that original record. It's the thing you have to produce if anyone suspects you've been making things up about your age or your name. You might not carry it with you from day to day, but a huge amount of official machinery quietly depends on it being there.

You mostly run into it when you need to prove you are who you say you are. You can't get a driver's license, a passport, or get in to vote without it. Getting married is another place the state will want to see one, and some employers will ask for it. It is also the key you will need to get one issued for your own kids. Without it you are generally stuck, since it is the first document everything else gets pulled from. The only real trouble comes if you lose one, since getting a replacement takes a fair bit of time and paper work.

You will probably ignore it for the first few years of your life. It tends to jump into your face a bit later, mostly at the moments when you want to do something the government has put a foot on. Keeping a copy somewhere safe is a bit of trouble that pays off later on.

groups.question: How did the commonality of "seeing the light" originate when people are "crossing over" or passing away?
texts:
You are mostly running into a closed loop of story telling. You have a fairly small number of first person accounts, some going back further but the real collection of them mostly happening in the last seventy years or so. Doctors and authors have then latched onto these as a shared experience, and the repetition has made them seem far more common than the actual numbers would show. That sort of thing will naturally squelch or reshape the parts of the accounts that did not fit the emerging pattern.

You can get some explanation from what we know of the brain in extremis, since we have seen similar visions produced through other means. That said the fit is not perfect and the experiences reported have a great deal of similarity to the religious expectations of the person having them. It is probably closest to the truth to say that a number of people die, that a few of them report such a thing, and that a tradition has since grown up around those particular examples. You have gotten your sense of it being a universal rule almost entirely through that process.

You've almost certainly got it from a jumble of the visual cortex getting starved of blood in a very particular way. That part of the brain is laid out so that the kind of disruption you get in extremis maps onto a bright spot that seems to rise. Add in the fact that the thalamus stops filtering the rest of your sensory input, and you get an undifferentiated impression the mind is perfectly equipped to dress up as a light. From there the whole thing gets locked in by the stories you already have in your head. You end up experiencing your own neural failure in the only idiom you've been given. That is also why the reports look so alike across very different people. You are watching a neurological attractor state get described through a very well established set of ideas.

None of that pins down what the thing actually feels like from the inside, since you would need to get that information back from someone whose brain was in the middle of failing. You are left with the outer shape of a very consistent account and a fair number of plausible things that could produce it. Neither of those by itself gets you to an answer.

You probably have two things tangled together. The near-death experience of seeing a bright light is remarkably consistent across wildly different cultures, and that consistency points to something in the brain's own machinery. When the visual cortex gets starved of oxygen it tends to produce that very bright light, and the way the rest of the brain organizes that input can look a lot like a tunnel. You get the same general result whether the cause is a heart attack or a fall, because the underlying neural conditions are similar. That religious story of a soul passing through into another state got wrapped around this biological experience, and the two got so thoroughly mixed that they are now hard to tell apart.

People who have had this experience and come back to tell it are essentially reporting the same thing, whether they grew up in an environment that gave that thing a spiritual name or not. You can pretty much explain the shape of the experience without any of the religious framework. The framework is the part that got added on top. You would find the same reports, though probably without the same vocabulary, in a lot of places where that particular set of religious ideas is entirely absent.

You are seeing a shared biological event that cultures then dress up in their own religious language. Kids who haven't yet absorbed a full death narrative report the same basic experience, which is pretty strong evidence the source is internal. The temporal lobe produces bright visual images under enough electrical stimulation, and that same area is prone to misfire when the brain is short on oxygen. You then get a brain that is already hungry for some kind of story to make sense of what it is feeling. Since nearly every tradition on record has some version of a luminous presence, the result is a very consistent set of reports. The light isn't actually agreed upon in advance, it is that the underlying mechanism is so uniform.

That said the people who have gone through it are understandably inclined to read their own set of beliefs into the experience. You end up with a fact that is universal in its underlying cause but wildly variable in the meaning that gets assigned to it.

You get most of the shape you are asking about from one guy, Raymond Moody, who put out a book in 1975 called Life After Life. Before that you could find bits and pieces of it here and there, in older mystical traditions for instance, but nobody had bothered to collect them or write them up in the way he did. He took a whole lot of unrelated stories and forced them into that single sequence of tunnel, light, and return. The book took off and pretty much froze that version in place. You are now getting it back in the movies and television shows that have followed.

That said, this particular flavor of the story isn't all that universal. When you look at the accounts that do get recorded in other places, the light tends to get read in ways that are very particular to the local set of beliefs. A lot of people want to take that as proof of some common human hardware, though the whole thing looks a lot more like a modern invention that got very good at dressing itself in the clothes of the oldest stories.

You are mostly getting that from the religious stories that were already in circulation. Christianity, Islam, and a number of other faiths had a pretty standard account of the dead going to a bright, good place, so a person in a delirium was perfectly capable of fitting in with that. The New Testament lays it out pretty clearly and the Koran does much the same thing. You get a bit of that kind of thing in the Tibetan accounts as well. That gave people a ready made explanation for what they were seeing. You can also see plenty of medical research that points to the visual cortex lighting up very heavily while the rest of the brain is shutting down. That sort of phenomenon happens in the wake of anoxia. You end up with the two sets of explanations getting so thoroughly mixed that it is hard to pick one from the other.

You also have to keep in mind that the reports of that sort of thing have been going on for a very long time. You find them in lots of early medical literature where the doctor in question had no religious axe to grind. That helps to show that the experience itself is not necessarily the result of any particular set of beliefs. How a person ends up making sense of the experience is where the cultural differences start to show up.

It's mostly the long time Christians had at picture making. The whole map of the afterlife got drawn with the saved ending up in brightness and the damned going off in the dark. You see it in the frescoes, the painted panels, and Dante's very influential arrangement of things. The安排 got so thoroughly worked over that the two ended up standing as shorthand for the two outcomes. You didn't need to elaborate. Saying a person had seen the light told you which way they had gone.

That picture then made it easier to read a dying person's actual reports. A fair number of them describe a bright glow at the edge of what they can see, and the people sitting by took that in through the same ready made lens. The two things, the old symbolic map and the reports of the actual experience, wound up feeding into each other. You can find the expression in that sense in the sermons and popular literature of the middle part of the last several hundred years, but it is doing mostly the job that the scriptures themselves had started.

You will get light and dark opposed to each other in a good many other traditions as well, though. Getting the particular construction you have in the habit of using takes you back to that more bounded set of influences.

You're kind of getting two different things that got braided together. The visual part has a pretty straightforward explanation in the brain. When oxygen runs out, the central part of the visual field keeps working a little longer while the periphery goes out. That leaves a bright spot in the middle of a dark tunnel, and the brain will happily read that as a light. You can get the same effect by pressing on your eyes. The tunnel shape is just what that kind of visual contraction looks like.

The story you've heard is a much more recent development. Different cultures have taken that same basic visual input and built very different things around it. The version that includes the light at the end, the super peaceful feeling, and the familiar people you meet got standardized in a single 1975 book by a psychologist. Before that the accounts were far more mixed. That book did more to shape the experience than any of the experiences did.

It also matters that you are only getting reports from people who were brought back. Nobody actually knows what, if anything, happens to those who aren't. The whole picture you have got to be a fairly recent and pretty well shaped cultural product laid over top of something that was going on in the brain all along.

groups.question: What is the speed of electricity?
texts:
It's two different things you're getting mixed up. The information you're sending down a wire, like the command to turn a light on, moves at a pretty good clip, something like two thirds of the speed of light. That's why the whole thing happens to your eyes in an instant. The electrons along that same wire are progressing in the general direction of that signal at a snail's pace, amounting to only a few millimeters per second. You can picture it pretty well by watching a long file of people who all turn around at once when a shout reaches the end of the line. What moves fast is the shout, not the people.

You might change that first figure by changing the material you run the line in since different things handle the passing along of such signals in different degrees. A vacuum gets you the full speed of light, and many of the insulating materials found in modern wiring lag quite a bit behind. The slow crawl on the part of the electrons isn't affected by all that to any worth noticing.

You are probably thinking of two different things that get lumped together. The signal that carries the energy races down a wire at roughly 50 to 99 percent of the speed of light. The specific number comes down to what insulating material you put around it, with teflon getting you closer to light speed than, say, oil. The actual electrons in the copper are going some thing like a millimeter a second in their random wanderings. They get jostled along by that fast moving signal but they themselves are barely getting anywhere. That is why you see a light go on practically the instant you throw a switch.

You will get a bit different of a number if you are looking at a submarine cable than you do in the wiring of your own home. The paraffin used in the sea has more of an effect on the overall speed than the various plastics around in a building. Still, it ends up being a large enough share of the fastest speed in the universe.

It depends on what part of the business you are looking at. The signal that carries power and information moves along the wire at a large fraction of the speed of light. You will get somewhere between 50 and 99 percent of that 186,000 miles per second figure. The particular percentage is mostly a function of the insulating material you have around the conductor. That is the part you see when you flip a switch and a light comes on.

The electrons themselves are moving at a snail's pace in comparison. In a copper wire they will only manage a fraction of a millimeter per second. You are getting the effect almost instantly because the push on those electrons gets transmitted down the line at the much faster signal speed. Think of it like the way a long string of marbles will move almost as fast as the one you push at the other end.

For most of the practical effects you run into day to day the signal speed is the one that matters. You will get effectively the same result on a short run of wire as you would if that signal were able to move at the full speed of light.

You are probably getting two different numbers mixed up. The energy or signal that makes a light turn on races along the wire at 2/3 to 6/7 of the speed of light, which is fast enough to be essentially instantaneous in a house. The little electrons you'd find in that same wire actually barely get anywhere, drifting along at something like a tenth of a millimeter per second. You can get a feel for it by looking at a long cable for a pair of flashlights at either end, where that near light speed propagation shows up as a very small but measurable delay. The actual fraction of light you get changes with the insulation the wire is wrapped in.

You would reach a different conclusion if you were dealing with something like a superconducting circuit, though for pretty much every day to day purpose the 2/3 figure holds up.

You get two very different numbers depending on what you mean. The electrons themselves barely get anywhere, sort of drifting along at a millimeter or two per second. That slow shuffle is what carries the actual charge. The signal out in front of them, the electric field that makes the whole thing work, zooms along at 60 to 90 percent of the speed of light. You are watching that signal when you see a distant light come on the instant you flip a switch.

groups.question: Why are death row inmates housed separately?
texts:
You get a fair mix of security and legal reasons out of it. If they were in the general population the odds of someone getting killed by other inmates go way up, which would just tie up the courts even more. The whole legal machine from that first appeal right on through to the final order also runs a lot more smoothly when it isn't getting tangled up in the daily business of a regular penitentiary. Getting them out to the place of execution is a mostly separate matter as well. You will find the same basic isolationist strategy used to handle other populations that the authorities view as extreme risks.

The living conditions that result from all that separation are pretty grim in most places. That part is more the inevitable byproduct of the system than anything that was originally set out to be achieved. Most of the time the people pushing for it aren't particularly concerned with that aspect of the arrangement.

It's mostly a security matter. Inmates who have been sentenced to death pose what the systems they're in judge to be a higher escape risk, and they need a level of supervision the general population wings aren't set up to provide. Keeping them in their own units also stops the wider prison from being politically or psychologically influenced by that group. The practical upshot is a lot of time in cells with very limited contact with other people. That level of isolation ends up being one of the most damaging features of the setup, but removing it would undermine the security posture the whole thing is built on. You get a system that is very hard to compromise and very hard to endure at the same time.

You'll see different versions of all this from one state to another. Some use entirely self contained complexes while others just set aside a heavily guarded wing of an existing prison. The underlying calculation about risk and control is pretty much the same in all the cases.

It's mostly about keeping the whole thing from falling apart. If you put them in the general population the other guys are bound to try to get even for some offense, real or imagined. That isn't some wild possibility, it happens in enough places to make the gamble impossible. At the same time you need to keep the inmates from getting outside help with an escape or from being able toinfluence the others. A lot of the specific rules you see are just the states trying to get ahead of the kinds of court challenges that have already forced them to change things. You end up paying out in the form of a lot of extra staff and very closely watched routines to keep a bad situation from getting worse.

People who look at it from the outside sometimes get hung up on the moral questions, but the people actually running the place have simply got to handle the very immediate threats that are present in the situation. It works out to be a set of precautions that the other model for handling the situation has been shown to be unable to provide.

Most of it comes down to keeping them from the general population. They've been found to have committed crimes the system considers beyond all other, and you don't want other inmates taking it out on them. That same reasoning goes for the inmates' own families or people who want in on them. Then you've got the legal side to work around. The whole appeal process can run for years, and you need a setup that keeps that process from getting tangled up with the rest of the institution. A separate unit makes all that easier to keep track of and keep separate.

The heavy use of solitary that people focus on is mostly a result of that first requirement rather than something the system set out to do. You can't put that many people with that particular legal standing together in a shared setting and still keep everyone else secure.

You get a bit of all of it. The first order of business is that the people who got you there are probably still around, and you don't want a run on you. The appeals in that kind of case outlast pretty much everything else you'd see in the system, sometimes for decades. Lumping everyone in that boat together keeps the whole thing from sprawling out into the rest of the prison. That general crowd is also a lot more at ease knowing they are kept out of it.

That segregation ends up doing a good deal of psychological work on its own. You aren't getting any extra punishment for it so much as you are being kind of locked out of any of the normal things that might wear that sort of thing off. It is a lot of trouble and money to keep up, to be sure, but the system seems to figure that is a price it has to pay.

It comes down to a few practical problems you'd run into in a regular unit. You can't let other inmates get at the witnesses who will testify against the prisoner, and you've got to keep the outside world from getting in to get at them. That last part covers everything from potential rescues to attempts to tamper with the legal proceedings. The separate housing also keeps the whole operation from getting out, since word of a specific date or plan would have to go through a much smaller and more easily controlled group of people. How much of that gets applied in practice depends on the state, though.

You'll also find a fair amount of extra psychological monitoring in these units. Some of it is there to keep an eye on any signs of self harm, but a good deal of it also ends up being testimony in the eventual legal battles over the sentence.

You need a pretty clear answer to whether the person you're going to kill is still you. If other prisoners can get at him a successful kidnapping or murder would end the whole case and start it over. That last part is the big one though. Any time an inmate got into a fight or got in some other kind of trouble it would generate a fresh batch of legal challenges to block a sentence. Keeping them in a single, fully controlled unit stops that whole mess from getting in the way of the end of the process. The only real snag is that that kind of total control turns out to be a lot of permanent solitary confinement, which is its own sort of problem.

You are looking at a system that got so caught up in its own logic it ended up justifying the worst of what it was actually doing. The safety concerns that got it started are now mostly there to keep the present arrangement from getting looked at.

You get a few different things out of it. The obvious one is that you can't just put people who are scheduled to be killed in with the general population. They'd be in a lot of trouble fast. The system also needs to keep the whole process from getting tampered with, and that's a lot easier to do in a closed off unit. Outsiders can't get in, the inmates can't get out, and the whole thing becomes easier to control for the appeals process. That process could drag out for years.

You also get a side effect that a bunch of the facilities have just ended up accepting. The isolation is so complete that it starts to break people's heads. The whole thing isn't so much a well thought out policy as it is a collection of answers to separate institutional problems. Those answers all happen to point the same way. Where that leaves the people ends up being an afterthought.
