groups.question: How people program "Angry Birds"-like physics and collision detection.
texts:
You are almost certainly running on top of a general purpose 2D rigid body solver. Angry Birds itself was built on Box2D, which is still the go to for the genre. You describe your world in terms of simple static bodies for the terrain and a loose pile of rectangles for the structures. The birds and slingshot projectiles are just circles, which keeps the collision math fast and the edge cases predictable. You are not modeling a pig, you are modeling a handful of approximations that look like one.

Get the slingshot feel by simply setting a velocity vector on the bird when the player lets go. What makes the level work is then almost entirely a matter of tweaking the restitution and friction for each material. Ice blocks slide and shatter in a different way than a log because you have assigned them different parameters. The whole thing feels satisfying when those numbers are right and breaks down when they are not.

The satisfying destruction you see is a damage bookkeeping system bolted onto the real physics. You keep a running total of the impulse each block has taken and you stop it from being a physics body the moment that total gets too high. That is far more tractable for a game than trying to get the engine to simulate actual fracture. You will also find that the games lock their simulation to a fixed time step and only interpolate for the display. Letting that step vary with the frame rate lets a fast moving bird tunnel right through a thin wall.

You are almost certainly using a rigid body engine like Box2D that already has the intersection math done. You describe a pig as a circle and a tree house as a set of static and dynamic rectangles, and the engine takes it from there. It checks for overlapping shapes by first looking at a quick coarse bounding box, and only works out the exact intersection points for shapes that actually get close. That coarse to fine search is the only way you keep the frame rate up with a whole screen of physics objects.

The game design lives in the material properties you attach to those shapes. You set the density on the birds so they carry the force you want on impact and define a somewhat arbitrary damage threshold for the structures. When the engine reports a collision that clears that threshold you then run your own trigger logic to remove the damaged parts. The slingshot you see on the screen is just a set of constraints that you release with a recorded velocity to get the shot started. You end up tuning all those numbers through a lot of play testing since you are trying to keep the physics from looking completely fake while still letting the game play well.

That whole approach of leaning on a general purpose simulation and then bolting on the special cases is the standard way to get these games off the ground. You would only need to touch the underlying collision methods if you went for some very unusual shape that the off the shelf engine could not manage.

You mostly get away with not building your own engine. You lean on something like Box2D or Bullet and then map your game objects to the standard shapes those libraries understand. The slingshot works by making the bird a kinematic body while your finger is on it, and then on release you just calculate the distance it was pulled and fire off a corresponding impulse. That impulse is the only part you do yourself and the rest of the flight is left to the engine to sort out.

Getting the right feel for the different materials is mostly a matter of layering on extra rules. The engine hands you the speed and angle of an impact, and then your own code has to decide what happens. You keep a running total of that damage on every object and once it gets too much you simply delete the thing and let the resulting forces knock the rest of the pile over. It is that knockdown you are fighting to achieve that takes the most fiddling to get right.

You will run into a lot of trouble if you try to let the engine vary its internal time steps. It pays to run the whole thing on a lot of very small fixed steps to keep the pile from just exploding into the sky. Everything you actually see then gets built on top of that pretty headless mechanical result.

You mostly get the hard part for free. Box2D was literally the original engine under the first games, and it still handles the broad phase collision search and the narrow phase shape overlap tests. You wrap it in your own game logic. The slingshot is just a mouse joint that you apply a force to until the player lets go. Birds that do something special are scripted triggers attached to their collision shapes. That bit is nearly trivial.

The structural stuff is where you have to do your own work. You keep a running total of the impulse each block takes and let it go once that total crosses a limit. That limit is different for wood and ice and stone, and that is the entire trick behind the different gameplay they give you. Getting it to feel right takes a lot of fiddling with those numbers. You will almost certainly also hand tune the stacks you are building. The generic solver will not keep a tower perfectly still until something hits it.

The rest of the feel people remember comes from presentation. The way a block visibly cracks as it nears its failure point is just an animation you run off that same impulse total. None of it is actually in the underlying collision math.

You get almost all of it for free from an off the shelf 2D physics engine. The original game ran on Box2D, and most clones do the same. You set a global gravity value and let the engine handle the rest of the integration for you. The birds are just circles with a restitution and density you've tuned to get the bounce and penetration you want. The slingshot isn't really a physics feature either, you are simply setting the body's linear velocity to match the direction of your release.

The actual game play is mostly an exercise in how you assemble the levels. The wooden and stone structures are a bunch of very simple box colliders linked by revolute and weld joints. Those joints take a certain amount of force before they give way, and what you are playing to do is get a single impact to cascade through the whole thing. The pigs are little circle shapes with no joints at all so any bit of that cascading damage takes them out. You end up designing the whole thing by trial and error, watching to see if the parts you welded together are strong enough to survive the sort of hits you are likely to get.

You are mostly just bending a very standard projectile model to your needs. The slingshot gives you a vector that is the direction you pulled the bird, scaled by how far you pulled it. From that point the simulation is just gravity acting on that initial velocity, which you step forward frame by frame. You want to step the velocity first and then the position from that new velocity, or you will get a noticeable amount of extra energy on every step.

The collision part is you trying to make a number of cheap tests in sequence. First you check if the rough circular boundaries around the two bodies are far enough apart to ignore. For the cases that survive that test you look at the actual polygons to find the smallest overlapping distance. You push the two bodies apart along that distance, and then you split the change in velocity you have to give them between the two according to their mass.

You have to invent your own rules for what happens next. The game wants certain birds to be capable of taking out a whole tower on the first hit. That is not in the general case of those collision rules. You end up adding a damage tally that keeps track of the force involved in each contact. When that tally for a given block crosses a certain line you simply remove it from the simulation. You tune all of those lines by hand until the results agree with the feel you want.

You are almost certainly not writing the math yourself. The whole thing runs on a library like Box2D, which is a 2D rigid body solver built on impulse methods. You describe the birds and the terrain as collections of simple polygonal or circular shapes, and hand the library a table of masses and restitution values. It then marches the world forward in fixed timesteps, which the game loop drives at 60 or 120 per second. There is a broad phase that quickly culls any pairs that are far apart, and a much more expensive narrow phase that checks the exact geometry of the rest.

The slingshot is just a point to point constraint that you apply and then cut at the moment the bird leaves your finger. The destructible cliffs work by building them out of many small blocks, some of which the engine can freely destroy while others remain static. You get most of that jingly feel by setting the engine to run its resolution calculations over several extra iterations during each timestep. More of those passes generally means the birds bounce off each other in a more satisfying way, at the price of a bit more CPU time.

You will end up spending almost all of your time on that last point. The underlying collision detection is fine out of the box, but the game is what you make of it by fiddling with the iteration counts and the material properties you assign to each of the bodies.

You get almost the whole thing from impulse based solvers that run every frame. The birds and slingshot work on a simple parabolic path until something gets in the way. The walls and pigs are made out of box and convex polygon colliders that those circles slam into.

You drive the destruction off of the accumulated impulse at the point of contact. A bird that clips a corner does not hit hard enough to take a piece of it down but a full frontal hit will. That value gets compared to a material specific strength to decide if the object should break into a few pre made pieces. The fragments for those broken pieces are just further circles and boxes that go back into the solver so they can keep knocking things over. You are not simulating continuous fracture, just a lot of very convincing looking breakage.

The whole thing ends up being a fairly loose interpretation of real world physics. You can fake a lot of the tricky bits because the game only needs to look and feel right to a person who is trying to take down a castle in a few tries.

groups.question: What makes the F-14 so loved and the F-35 so hated?
texts:
It is mostly a matter of what kind of product you are looking at. When you bought or watched the F 14 you had a finished article in front of you. That thing worked out, it was fast, and it looked the part. You got to enjoy that finish without having to put up with the endless problems that have plagued the thing it has ended up replacing. Put a number of good movies on top of that and you end up with something that has been able to keep a certain romantic hold on the public.

The F 35 has never had much of a chance to get in any kind of good position with the public. You get to see it through a series of delays, a huge amount of extra cost, and bugs that have never quite got worked out. That is pretty much all you see. You are asked to take on faith that the thing will eventually pull together in some way.

That sort of thing ends up putting you in a position of having to settle for a good memory in place of a working machine. That is about the extent of it.

You've got a war movie to thank for the F 14. Top Gun came out right when people wanted a scrub hero story, and the pictures in it showed the plane doing things that were mostly true. That got locked in as the only story that mattered. You have to add in the fact that the plane was built around a specific cold war threat that just happened to go away. Nostalgia filled in the rest of the picture nicely.

The F 35 has been handed the job of replacing a whole bunch of different types at once. That meant the public got to read an unbroken stream of genuine and well documented problems for years on end. Nobody is going to put together a war movie to rescue that record. You get the very same thing if you look around the airline world, where people will happily romanticize some far more limited older contraption. The two planes ended up on opposite sides of the public story because of what that story happened to become.

You mostly got to see the F-14 at the end of its story. By the time it was a household name it had already got to be a clean part of a legend, polished up by Top Gun and the like. You never got to watch it crash out in its first decade. The F 35 is still in the middle of its own story and that story keeps putting out new cost overruns and technical glitches for the public to latch onto. You are watching the ugly middle of the process instead of the clean result.

The roles don't help either. The F 14 sold a nice old time vision of the fighter pilot as some sort of feudal knight flying an over the horizon spear. The F 35 is mostly a flying sensor system with the whole warfighting picture cooked up in the back. That is much harder for people to get behind on an emotional level.
